Every page of the graxia packages in full. Relative links inside a page are relative to the source path printed above it.

# @graxia/core — @graxia/core

Source: packages/core/README.md

# @graxia/core

The Bun-native GraphQL server engine: typed plugins, graphql 17, GraphQL over HTTP, with no
adapter layer. Pass a schema, get a `fetch` handler that follows the
[GraphQL over HTTP](https://graphql.github.io/graphql-over-http/) spec (it passes every
`graphql-http` server audit).

> Pre-1.0: the API is settling. Expect minor versions to change it, with the change in the
> changelog; pin a minor until 1.0.

## Requirements

- [Bun](https://bun.sh) 1.4.4 or later (the `engines` field). No Node or Deno adapter.
- `graphql` `^17.1.0`, as a peer dependency (17.1.0 is the version the suite runs against).
- `@softistx/telemetry` `^0.4.1` is an optional peer: with it installed graxia emits spans,
  without it tracing is off (see [Telemetry](#telemetry)).
- `typescript` is an optional peer, for types. Use `"moduleResolution": "bundler"` in your
  `tsconfig.json`. `nodenext` resolves the published declarations too (the release build checks
  both resolutions), but the sources are written for a bundler.

## Install

```sh
bun add @graxia/core graphql@^17
bun add @softistx/telemetry  # optional, enables spans
```

The snippets below reuse the `graxia` and `schema` of the quick start instead of repeating them.

## Quick start

```ts
import { createGraxia, createSchema } from '@graxia/core';

const schema = createSchema()({
	typeDefs: 'type Query { hello(name: String = "world"): String }',
	resolvers: { Query: { hello: (_root, { name }) => `hello ${name}` } },
});

const graxia = createGraxia({ schema });
graxia.serve({ port: 3000 }); // POST or GET http://localhost:3000/graphql
```

```sh
curl -s localhost:3000/graphql -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"query":"{ hello(name: \"Ada\") }"}'
# {"data":{"hello":"hello Ada"}}
```

To keep your own `Bun.serve` and routes, mount the handler: `Bun.serve({ fetch: graxia.fetch })`.
Details in [GraphQL over HTTP](./docs/guide/http.md).

## Plugins

A plugin is a plain object with a `name` and the hooks it needs (`onRequest`, `onParams`,
`onParse`, `onValidate`, `onContext`, `onExecute`, `onResponse`, ...). Returning a function from a
hook runs it after the stage (except `onContext` and `onResponse`, which have no
after-hook; `onResponse` replaces the response with `setResponse`). A plugin may also declare
`csrfExempt(request)` for its own `GET` requests (see [Security](./docs/guide/security.md)); for an
in-browser explorer see `@graxia/graphiql`.

```ts
import { createGraxia, definePlugin } from '@graxia/core';

const timing = definePlugin({
	name: 'timing',
	onRequest: () => {
		const start = performance.now();
		return () => console.log(`took ${performance.now() - start}ms`);
	},
});

createGraxia({ schema, plugins: [timing] });
```

A plugin that reads something from the context declares it with the curried form,
`definePlugin<{ request: Request }>()({ ... })`, so `onContext` still infers what it adds. See
[Plugins](./docs/guide/plugins.md) and its [Typed context](./docs/guide/plugins.md#typed-context) section.

## Context, written once

The `context` option builds one context per operation. Write it once, derive its type with
`InferContext`, and resolvers get it as their third argument. `createGraxia` then checks, at compile
time, that the schema's context is what the factory, the plugins and graxia provide.

```ts
import {
	type ContextInit,
	createGraxia,
	createSchema,
	type InferContext,
} from '@graxia/core';

const context = async ({ request }: ContextInit) => ({
	user: await authenticate(request), // { id: string } | null
});
type Ctx = InferContext<typeof context>; // { user: … } & { signal: AbortSignal }

const schema = createSchema<Ctx>()({
	typeDefs: 'type Query { me: String }',
	resolvers: { Query: { me: (_, __, ctx) => ctx.user?.id } },
});

const graxia = createGraxia({ schema, context }); // a missing or wrong key is a type error

// Stop cleanly: drains in-flight operations, answers 503 to new ones.
process.on('SIGTERM', () => graxia.dispose());
```

Plugins that add context go in the second parameter, `InferContext<typeof context, typeof plugins>`.
Every context also carries a `signal` that aborts when the client leaves or the server shuts down;
`getContext()` reads the context from code far below a resolver. See
[Context, cancellation and shutdown](./docs/guide/context.md).

## Errors

Throw `exposedError` to show an error to the client; anything else is masked as
`Unexpected error.` with a correlation id equal to the `x-request-id` header.

```ts
import { createGraxia, createSchema, exposedError } from '@graxia/core';

const schema = createSchema()({
	typeDefs: 'type Query { book(id: ID!): String }',
	resolvers: {
		Query: {
			book: (_root, args) => {
				throw exposedError('NOT_FOUND', `No book ${String(args.id)}.`, {
					fix: 'Check the id.',
				});
			},
		},
	},
});

createGraxia({
	schema,
	onUnexpected: (error, { correlationId }) =>
		console.error(correlationId, error), // the original error, for your logs
});
```

See [Errors](./docs/guide/errors.md).

## Limits and caches

Here `graxia` is the instance from the quick start. Documents are parsed under token and nesting limits, operations are refused over
a depth, alias, directive, root field or cost limit (all on by default), and parsed and validated documents are cached.
See [Security](#security).

```ts
createGraxia({
	schema,
	limits: {
		tokens: 15_000,
		nesting: 1_000,
		bodyBytes: 1_048_576,
		depth: 12,
		aliases: 30,
		directives: 50,
		rootFields: 20,
		cost: { max: 5_000 }, // @cost / @listSize; `false` turns a limit off
	},
	caches: { parse: { max: 1024, ttlMs: 3_600_000 } }, // or `false`
	batching: { limit: 10 }, // off by default
});
```

See [Limits and caches](./docs/guide/limits-and-caches.md).

## Security

graxia is a transport and plugin engine, not a hardened edge. What it does, and what it does not:

**On by default**

- Error masking: a resolver error that is not an `exposedError` or a `GraphQLError` reaches the
  client as `Unexpected error.` with a correlation id; the original goes to `onUnexpected`.
- A request body limit (`limits.bodyBytes`, 1 MiB; more answers 413).
- Document limits before parsing: at most 15 000 tokens and 1 000 nesting levels
  (`limits.tokens`, `limits.nesting`); a failure is `GRAPHQL_PARSE_FAILED`.
- Operation limits: depth 12, 30 aliases, 50 directives, 20 root fields and a cost of 5 000
  (`limits.depth`, `.aliases`, `.directives`, `.rootFields`, `.cost`), fragments expanded; a refusal is
  `GRAPHQL_VALIDATION_FAILED` with `extensions.limit`. Cost follows `@cost` / `@listSize`, which
  `createSchema` adds to your SDL (`costDirectives` does for a schema you build yourself);
  `computeOperationCost` returns an operation's cost for plugins and tests.
- Batching is off unless you set `batching: { limit }`.
- A client's `x-request-id` is never trusted or echoed; graxia generates the id.
- Server-sent events and WebSocket (`subscriptions.sse`, `subscriptions.ws`) are on, on the endpoint's
  path; turn either off with `false`.
- CSRF prevention: a request a browser can send cross-site without a preflight (a `GET`, or a
  `POST` with a `text/plain`, form or multipart body) is refused with 403 unless it carries one of
  `DEFAULT_CSRF_HEADERS` (`x-graphql-csrf`, `graphql-require-preflight`,
  `apollo-require-preflight`, `x-apollo-operation-name`). A JSON `POST` needs nothing.
- WebSocket origin check: an upgrade whose `Origin` is `null` or another site's is refused with
  403; list the browser origins that may connect in `csrf.sameOrigin.allowedOrigins`.
- Introspection and "Did you mean" suggestions are on in development and off when
  `NODE_ENV=production` (`introspection`, `suggestions`).

```ts
createGraxia({
	schema,
	csrf: { sameOrigin: { allowedOrigins: ['https://app.example.com'] } }, // also checks Origin over HTTP
	introspection: false,
});
```

See [Security](./docs/guide/security.md) for client setup, the `sameOrigin` modes and `NODE_ENV`.
A plugin that serves its own `GET` page (such as the GraphiQL explorer of `@graxia/graphiql`) can exempt it from the header with `csrfExempt`; core still refuses an exempt request no plugin answers.

**Opt-in**

- Trusted documents (`trustedDocuments`): see below.
- Field rate limits (`fieldRateLimit`): see below.

Rate-limit the endpoint as a whole in a proxy or gateway.

## Rate limiting fields

Limit how often a client selects chosen fields, counted across aliases and fragments (three aliased
`signIn` in one request spend 3 units). Past a limit nothing executes: `429` with `Retry-After`.

```ts
import { createGraxia, fieldRateLimit, memoryFieldLimit } from '@graxia/core';

createGraxia({
	schema,
	plugins: [
		fieldRateLimit({
			fields: {
				signIn: {
					limit: memoryFieldLimit({ limit: 5, windowMs: 60_000 }),
					single: true,
				},
			},
			// key: (ctx) => ctx.userId, ipv6Prefix: 64, code: 'RATE_LIMITED'
		}),
	],
});
```

`single: true` also refuses the field selected twice in one operation (`400`,
`FIELD_SELECTED_ONCE`). The default key is the client address `serve()` read; give `key` behind a
proxy or with `fetch()`. Use `redisFieldLimit` from `@graxia/redis` to share the limit across processes. See
[Rate limiting fields](./docs/guide/rate-limiting.md).

## Telemetry

Install `@softistx/telemetry` (an optional peer) and an exporter (`@softistx/telemetry-otlp` for an
OTLP backend), then `createTelemetry(...).install()`: graxia emits spans for each request, parse,
validation and operation, and the original exception of an unexpected error. Without the peer,
nothing is wrapped and nothing runs.

```ts
createGraxia({ schema, telemetry: { resolverSpans: true } }); // or `telemetry: false`
```

Setup, the span tree, attributes, every option and the migration from `@opentelemetry/api`:
[Telemetry](./docs/guide/telemetry.md).

## Trusted documents

Let production run only the documents your clients ship: a manifest (Relay, graphql-codegen or
Apollo format), `documentId`, automatic persisted queries and a strict mode.

```ts
createGraxia({
	schema,
	trustedDocuments: {
		manifest: await Bun.file('persisted-documents.json').json(),
		// mode: 'strict' when NODE_ENV=production, 'mixed' otherwise
		// store: redisCache({ url }) shares APQ registrations across processes
	},
});
// POST { "documentId": "a3f1..." }, GET ?documentId=..., or an APQ hash in extensions.persistedQuery
```

In `strict` a query sent in full is refused with `PERSISTED_QUERY_ONLY`. Without the option nothing
changes. See [Trusted documents](./docs/guide/trusted-documents.md).

## Production

Set `NODE_ENV=production`: introspection and "Did you mean" hints go off, trusted documents run in
`strict` mode, and the unexpected-error log goes quiet. Masked errors, CSRF checks, operation
limits, no batching and a server-made request id are on in every environment. Give
`trustedDocuments` your manifest, share the rate-limit and PubSub state across instances, set
`csrf.sameOrigin.allowedOrigins` and call `graxia.dispose()` on `SIGTERM`. The
[production guide](./docs/guide/production.md) has the full configuration and a checklist.

## `execute`

Run an operation in process (`graxia` is the instance from the quick start), through the same pipeline as HTTP (plugins, context, masking), for
tests, jobs and scripts.

```ts
const { data, errors } = await graxia.execute({
	document: 'query Greet($name: String) { hello(name: $name) }',
	variables: { name: 'Ada' },
	headers: { authorization: 'Bearer test' },
});
```

With `trustedDocuments`, `graxia.execute({ documentId, variables })` runs a persisted document by
id (without it the result is `Must provide a query string.`).

It rejects with a `GraxiaExecuteError` when a plugin answered with its own response (a 401, for
example) instead of a result. See [Testing](./docs/guide/testing.md).

The instance also exposes `graxia.schema` (the schema it serves) and `graxia.limits`
(`{ bodyBytes, tokens }`, defaults applied), so a layer in front of it, such as an MCP server,
needs neither passed twice, and `graxia.trustedDocuments` (`{ mode }` in force, or `undefined`).

## Testing client

`graxia` is the instance from the quick start. `@graxia/core/testing` sends requests through `graxia.fetch` with real HTTP semantics, without a
socket and without importing a test runner.

```ts
import { createTestClient, expectNoErrors } from '@graxia/core/testing';

const client = createTestClient(graxia, {
	headers: { 'x-request-source': 'test' },
});
const result = await client.query<{ hello: string }>('{ hello }');
expectNoErrors(result);
result.status; // 200
result.data?.hello; // 'hello world'
```

## Ready for agents

`@graxia/core/agent` adds descriptive `@needs`, `@constraint` and `@errors` directives, prints the schema one caller may see, and lints descriptions. Every error graxia emits carries `extensions.fix`.

```ts
import {
	agentTypeDefs,
	lintDescriptions,
	printSchemaFor,
} from '@graxia/core/agent';

// createSchema()({ typeDefs: [agentTypeDefs, sdl], resolvers })
const sdl = printSchemaFor(schema, {
	can: (permission) => permissions.has(permission),
});
expect(lintDescriptions(schema)).toEqual([]); // in a spec
```

See [Ready for agents](./docs/guide/agent.md).

## Key-value cache

`KeyValueCache` (with `CacheSetOptions`) is a small asynchronous string store; `createMemoryCache` is the
in-process LRU implementation with a per-entry `ttlMs`. `redisCache` in `@graxia/redis` is the shared one.

```ts
import { createMemoryCache } from '@graxia/core';

const cache = createMemoryCache({ maxEntries: 500 });
await cache.set('greeting', 'hello', { ttlMs: 60_000 });
await cache.get('greeting'); // 'hello'
```

See [limits and caches](./docs/guide/limits-and-caches.md).

## PubSub

A typed in-memory PubSub for subscription resolvers. It lives in one process; for several
instances, `redisPubSub` from `@graxia/redis` implements the same interface.

```ts
import { createPubSub, createSchema } from '@graxia/core';

const pubsub = createPubSub<{ tick: [payload: number] }>();

// This `schema` is the one the subscription examples below use.
const schema = createSchema<{ signal: AbortSignal }>()({
	typeDefs: 'type Query { hello: String } type Subscription { tick: Int! }',
	resolvers: {
		Query: { hello: () => 'world' },
		Subscription: {
			tick: {
				subscribe: () => pubsub.subscribe('tick'),
				resolve: (n: number) => n,
			},
		},
	},
});

await pubsub.publish('tick', 1);
// Yoga's shape: `subscribe('post', id)`, `publish('post', id, payload)`, and
// `pipe(source, filter(keep), map(fn))` to wrap a subscription's source.
```

## Subscriptions

Subscriptions are served over server-sent events (`graphql-sse`, distinct connections mode) to any
request whose `Accept` prefers `text/event-stream`, on by default. `graxia.serve()` keeps the
connection open; a keep-alive comment is sent every 12 s (`subscriptions.sse.keepAliveMs`, `0` turns it off).

```ts
// server: `createGraxia({ schema })` with the PubSub example's `schema`; publish with `pubsub.publish('tick', 1)`
// client: bun add graphql-sse
import { createClient } from 'graphql-sse';

const client = createClient({ url: 'http://localhost:3000/graphql' });
for await (const result of client.iterate({
	query: 'subscription { tick }',
}))
	console.log(result.data);
```

`onSubscribe` and `onResultChunk` plugin hooks run on these streams. See
[Subscriptions](./docs/guide/subscriptions.md).

### Over WebSocket

`graphql-transport-ws` on Bun's WebSocket is on by default, on the same path, for the `graphql-ws`
client. `connectionParams` reach `onConnect` and the context; `dispose()` closes sockets with 1001.

```ts
const live = createGraxia({
	schema,
	subscriptions: {
		ws: {
			onConnect: ({ connectionParams }) => connectionParams?.token === 'secret',
		},
	},
});
live.serve({ port: 3000 }); // ws://localhost:3000/graphql

// your own Bun.serve:
//   fetch: (req, server) =>
//     live.isUpgrade(req) ? live.upgrade(req, server) : live.fetch(req, { server }),
//   websocket: live.websocket
```

The upgrade's `Origin` is checked by default; list the browser origins that may connect in `csrf.sameOrigin.allowedOrigins`: see [Security](#security).

See [Subscriptions over WebSocket](./docs/guide/websocket.md): auth, close codes, keep-alive, limits.

## `@defer` and `@stream`

Queries and mutations with `@defer` or `@stream` are delivered incrementally to a client that sends
`Accept: multipart/mixed` (or `text/event-stream`), on by default; any other `Accept` gets
`INCREMENTAL_NOT_SUPPORTED` (HTTP 400 under `application/graphql-response+json`, 200 under `application/json`). `incremental: { format: 'legacy' }` speaks the 2022-08 format older
clients read, `incremental: false` turns it off.

A client example with `meros` is in the [guide](./docs/guide/incremental.md#a-client).

**Running the schema elsewhere.** `createSchema` declares `@defer` and `@stream`, so graphql's plain
`execute` refuses its schemas; use graxia or `experimentalExecuteIncrementally`, or build with
`createSchema()({ typeDefs, resolvers, incremental: false })` (no incremental queries then).

## Exports

# @graxia/core — Ready for agents: `@graxia/core/agent`

Source: packages/core/docs/guide/agent.md

# Ready for agents: `@graxia/core/agent`

A schema an AI agent can read and act on needs four things: what each field requires, the limits of
each input, the errors each field may return, and a `fix` on every error. `@graxia/core/agent` adds
the first three as three descriptive directives, prints the schema an agent may see, and lints the
descriptions. It is a separate subpath: the root import stays lean.

```ts
import {
	agentTypeDefs,
	lintDescriptions,
	printSchemaFor,
	visibleSchema,
} from '@graxia/core/agent';
```

## The directives

```ts
import { createSchema } from '@graxia/core';
import { agentTypeDefs } from '@graxia/core/agent';

const schema = createSchema()({
	typeDefs: [
		agentTypeDefs,
		`
		"The API."
		type Query {
			"The books the caller may read."
			books(
				"Words the title contains."
				search: String @constraint(minLength: 2, maxLength: 80)
				"How many books to return."
				first: Int = 10 @constraint(min: 1, max: 100)
			): [Book!]! @errors(codes: ["BAD_USER_INPUT"])
			"Every member of the library."
			members: [Member!]! @needs(permission: "members:read")
		}
		"A book on a shelf."
		type Book { "The book identifier." id: ID! }
		"A person registered with the library."
		type Member @needs(permission: "members:read") { "The member identifier." id: ID! }
	`,
	],
	resolvers: {},
});
```

| directive                                                                                                                  | on                       | meaning                                                                                                                                                                |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `@needs(permission: String)` or `@needs(anyOf: [String!])`, repeatable                                                     | field, object, interface | The permission a caller needs, or any one of a list. Repeated: every `@needs` must hold (AND).                                                                         |
| `@constraint(minLength, maxLength, min, max, exclusiveMin, exclusiveMax, multipleOf, minItems, maxItems, pattern, format)` | argument, input field    | The limits of a value, for clients and agents (JSON Schema names: `minimum`, `maximum`, `exclusiveMinimum`, `exclusiveMaximum`, `multipleOf`, `minItems`, `maxItems`). |
| `@errors(codes: [String!]!)`                                                                                               | field                    | The `extensions.code` values the field may return.                                                                                                                     |

Give `@needs` exactly one of `permission` and `anyOf`. A use with both or neither is invalid: the
field stays hidden from every caller (it fails closed) and `lintDescriptions` reports `invalid-needs`.
`@needs(permission: "a") @needs(anyOf: ["b", "c"])` means `a` AND (`b` OR `c`).

They are **descriptive**: graxia does not enforce them. Enforce `@needs` in your resolvers or a
plugin, and validate inputs where you accept them. Enforcement is on the roadmap.

For a schema built in code, pass `agentDirectives` to `new GraphQLSchema({ directives })`, and put the
same information in `extensions` with `agentExtensions`:

```ts
import { GraphQLString } from 'graphql';
import { agentExtensions } from '@graxia/core/agent';

const field = {
	type: GraphQLString,
	extensions: agentExtensions({
		needs: ['books:write', { anyOf: ['books:admin', 'books:owner'] }],
		errors: 'CONFLICT', // a code, or an array of codes
	}),
};
```

## Reading them

```ts
import { constraintOf, errorsOf, needsOf } from '@graxia/core/agent';

needsOf(fieldOrType); // [['members:read']]: AND of any-of groups; [['a'], ['b', 'c']] is a AND (b OR c)
constraintOf(argOrInputField); // { minLength: 2, maxLength: 80 } or undefined
errorsOf(field); // ['BAD_USER_INPUT']
```

Each reads the directives (including those on `extend type`) and `extensions.graxia`.

## `printSchemaFor(schema, { can })` and `visibleSchema`

The SDL one caller may see. `visibleSchema(schema, { can })` returns the same view as a
`GraphQLSchema` (no resolvers; the agent directives kept), to validate or introspect against. `can(permission)` says whether they hold a permission; absent, everything
is visible.

```ts
const sdl = printSchemaFor(schema, {
	can: (permission) => principal.permissions.has(permission),
});
```

`can` is typed `Can`, exported from `@graxia/core/agent`: `(permission: string) => boolean`.

- A field or type whose `@needs` fails is removed. A type left without fields is removed, and so is
  every field that returns it, until nothing changes. A union loses removed members and goes when none is left.
- Types no kept root type reaches are dropped (also with no `can`). An object that no longer has the
  fields of an interface stops declaring it.
- An object that is kept still implements its interfaces: an interface field that a kept
  implementer lacks is hidden too, and an interface left without fields is removed.
- The view always has a valid `Query`. When no query field is visible, `Query` keeps one placeholder
  field, `_empty: Boolean`, described as "Placeholder: no query field is visible to this caller."
  Nothing visible prints that minimal schema, never `""`; `buildSchema` accepts it.
- It keeps descriptions, `@deprecated`, `@specifiedBy`, `@oneOf` and the applied `@needs`,
  `@constraint` and `@errors`, declares the agent directives it uses, and leaves out `@defer`,
  `@stream`, introspection and built-in scalars. `buildSchema(sdl)` accepts the result. Types come in
  the schema's own order.
- It walks the whole schema: call it once per kind of principal and keep the text, not once per request.

## `lintDescriptions(schema, options)`

```ts
import { expect, test } from 'bun:test';
import { lintDescriptions } from '@graxia/core/agent';
import { schema } from './schema';

const knownErrorCodes = ['BAD_USER_INPUT', 'CONFLICT', 'NOT_FOUND'];

test('the schema describes itself', () => {
	expect(lintDescriptions(schema, { knownErrorCodes })).toEqual([]);
});
```

It returns `{ coordinate, rule, message, fix }[]` sorted by coordinate (`Type`, `Type.field`,
`Type.field(arg:)`, `Enum.VALUE`, `Input.field`):

| rule                      | when                                                                                     |
| ------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `missing-description`     | a type, field, argument, enum value or input field has none (`require` turns a kind off) |
| `short-description`       | under `minLength` characters (12 by default)                                             |
| `name-only-description`   | it only says the name again (`The id.` on `id`)                                          |
| `unknown-error-code`      | an `@errors` code is not in `knownErrorCodes`                                            |
| `invalid-needs`           | a `@needs` gives both `permission` and `anyOf`, or neither                               |
| `mutation-without-errors` | a mutation has no `@errors`                                                              |

The last two run only when `knownErrorCodes` is set. A field that implements a described interface field inherits its description. Introspection types,
built-in scalars and directive definitions are skipped.

## The `fix` contract

Every error graxia emits carries `extensions.fix`, a short sentence saying what the client changes,
the same in development and in production. The full contract, which errors are stamped and which are
never touched, is in [Errors](./errors.md#the-fix-contract). Errors you create with `exposedError`
carry the `fix` you give them; write one, so an agent can recover.

# @graxia/core — Codegen

Source: packages/core/docs/guide/codegen.md

# Codegen

[graphql-codegen](https://the-guild.dev/graphql/codegen)'s `typescript` and `typescript-resolvers`
plugins type every resolver from your SDL. Resolvers keep the signature `(parent, args, context, info)`
of graphql-tools, Yoga and Apollo, so the generated `Resolvers` type goes to `createSchema` as its
second generic. Graxia compiles the real output of both plugins in its own tests (a fixture with a
query, a mutation, subscriptions with and without `resolve`, an interface, a union, a custom scalar,
an enum with internal values and a mapper).

## Install and run

```sh
bun add -d @graphql-codegen/cli @graphql-codegen/typescript @graphql-codegen/typescript-resolvers
bunx graphql-codegen
```

## codegen.ts

Point `contextType` at the context written once with [`InferContext`](./context.md), so the resolver
context is never declared twice:

```ts
// src/context.ts
import { type ContextInit, type InferContext } from '@graxia/core';

export const plugins = [
	/* your plugins */
] as const;

export const context = async ({ request }: ContextInit) => ({
	user: await authenticate(request),
});
export type AppContext = InferContext<typeof context, typeof plugins>;
```

```ts
// codegen.ts: `schema` and `generates` paths are relative to the working directory;
// `contextType` and the `mappers` / `enumValues` modules are relative to the generated file.
import type { CodegenConfig } from '@graphql-codegen/cli';

const config: CodegenConfig = {
	schema: './schema.graphql',
	generates: {
		'./src/generated.ts': {
			plugins: ['typescript', 'typescript-resolvers'],
			config: {
				contextType: './context#AppContext',
				useTypeImports: true,
				// what resolvers return: the database row, not the GraphQL type
				mappers: { User: './models#UserRow' },
				// the enum's internal values
				enumValues: { Role: { ADMIN: 'admin', MEMBER: 'member' } },
				scalars: { Date: 'Date' },
			},
		},
	},
};
export default config;
```

## Passing `Resolvers` to `createSchema`

```ts
import { createGraxia, createSchema } from '@graxia/core';
import { context, plugins, type AppContext } from './context';
import type { Resolvers } from './generated';

const resolvers: Resolvers = {
	Query: { me: (_parent, _args, ctx) => ctx.user },
	User: { joined: (user) => new Date(user.at) },
	Subscription: {
		clock: {
			subscribe: async function* () {
				yield { clock: 1 };
			},
		},
	},
};

const schema = createSchema<AppContext, Resolvers>()({ typeDefs, resolvers });
createGraxia({ schema, context, plugins }).serve({ port: 3000 });
```

`createSchema` refuses a resolver map generated for another context than `AppContext` (the
`resolvers` option fails with `Property ''createSchema<Ctx>: these resolvers expect another context (see expected)'' is missing`; see [Troubleshooting](../troubleshooting.md)). Resolver
functions annotated with a different context are refused by the generated types themselves.

## Notes

- **Mappers** and **enumValues** work as in any server: graxia sets an enum's internal values from
  the `Role` resolver and returns whatever the resolvers return, the mapper type included.
- **Enums mapped to an external module** (`enumValues: { Role: './models#RoleValue' }`) make
  codegen emit `export { Role }` over a type-only import, which fails under
  `verbatimModuleSyntax`. Give the values inline, as above.
- **`resolve` of a subscription** receives the event typed `any` by codegen: annotate it
  (`resolve: (event: { title: string }) => ...`).
- The generated file is regenerated by you, not by `build`. Commit it.

## Coming from Yoga / Apollo

| You write                                       | In graxia                                                 |
| ----------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| `(parent, args, context, info) => ...`          | the same, `context` is your `InferContext` type           |
| `{ subscribe, resolve }`                        | the same                                                  |
| `__resolveType`, `__isTypeOf`                   | the same                                                  |
| `new GraphQLScalarType({ ... })`                | the same, under the scalar's name                         |
| `{ RED: 1 }` for an enum                        | the same                                                  |
| `makeExecutableSchema({ typeDefs, resolvers })` | `createSchema<Ctx, Resolvers>()({ typeDefs, resolvers })` |
| `context` factory in `createYoga`               | `context` option of `createGraxia`                        |

# @graxia/core — Context, cancellation and shutdown

Source: packages/core/docs/guide/context.md

# Context, cancellation and shutdown

Every operation gets its own context, its own cancellation signal, and is tracked so that
`dispose()` can drain it.

## How the context is built

For each operation (each entry of a batch included), in this order:

1. `serverContext`: what the host passed, `graxia.fetch(request, serverContext)`, or `{ server }`
   (Bun's server) when started with `graxia.serve()`.
2. The `context` option, merged over it: `{ ...serverContext, ...(await context(init)) }`.
3. The `onContext` plugin hooks, each merging what it returns.
4. `signal`, set last, always the operation's own signal.

The object is built again for every operation and never shared: a batch of three entries runs
with three contexts, so a plugin or resolver that mutates its context cannot leak into a sibling.

## Write the context once

Declare the factory, derive the type from it, and use that type for the schema. The resolver's
third argument is the context, typed.

```ts
import {
	type ContextInit,
	createGraxia,
	createSchema,
	definePlugin,
	type InferContext,
} from '@graxia/core';

const tenant = definePlugin({
	name: 'tenant',
	onContext: ({ request }) => ({
		tenant: request.headers.get('x-tenant') ?? 'public',
	}),
});
const plugins = [tenant] as const;

const context = async ({ request }: ContextInit) => ({
	user: await authenticate(request), // { id: string } | null
});

// { user: … } & { tenant: string } & { signal: AbortSignal }
type Ctx = InferContext<typeof context, typeof plugins>;

const schema = createSchema<Ctx>()({
	typeDefs: 'type Query { whoami: String }',
	resolvers: {
		Query: { whoami: (_root, _args, ctx) => `${ctx.tenant}/${ctx.user?.id}` },
	},
});

const graxia = createGraxia({ schema, context, plugins });
Bun.serve({ port: 3000, fetch: graxia.fetch });
```

`InferContext<Make, Plugins, HostCtx>` is what the factory returns (awaited), what the plugins add
(`ContextOf`, a tuple, so declare the list `as const` or inline), the `serverContext` type the
factory's `ContextInit<…>` declares, and what graxia always adds (`CoreContext`, the `signal`). Without a factory, use
`InferContext<undefined, typeof plugins>` or `InferContext` alone. `ContextFactory<HostCtx>` is the type of the
`context` option itself, for a factory declared apart from `createGraxia` (`const context: ContextFactory = …`).

### The host's `serverContext`

Annotate the factory with the host's type, `ContextInit<{ tenant: string }>`: `InferContext` reads
it, and `fetch`, `execute` and `serve` then require that `serverContext`. Never write
`createGraxia<…>`: an explicit type argument switches the context check off.

```ts
const context = ({
	request,
	serverContext,
}: ContextInit<{ tenant: string }>) => ({
	user: request.headers.get('x-user') ?? 'anonymous',
	tenant: serverContext.tenant,
});
type Ctx = InferContext<typeof context>; // { user: string; tenant: string; … }

const graxia = createGraxia({
	schema: createSchema<Ctx>()({ typeDefs, resolvers }),
	context,
});
Bun.serve({
	port: 3000,
	fetch: (request) => graxia.fetch(request, { tenant: 'acme' }),
});
```

### What the compiler checks

`createGraxia` compares the schema's `createSchema<Ctx>` type with the context it builds. Keys the
plugins, `serverContext` and graxia provide are taken into account; the rest must come from the
`context` factory.

- A `createSchema<Ctx>()` schema whose context needs a key nobody provides, or provides with another
  type, is a type error on `context` (a missing `context` option is "Property 'context' is missing").
- A plain `GraphQLSchema`, or `createSchema()` without `Ctx`, is not checked.
- A plugin list that is not a tuple (`GraxiaPlugin[]`) is not checked either.
- Do not write `createGraxia<…>`: an explicit type argument stops TypeScript inferring the others
  and turns the check off. Type the host on the factory, as above.

The errors are listed in [Troubleshooting](../troubleshooting.md).

`ContextInit` is `{ request, serverContext, params, signal }`.

## Cancellation: `signal`

Each operation has an `AbortSignal` that aborts when the client disconnects (`request.signal`) or
when `dispose()` gives up waiting (see below). It is `signal` in `ContextInit`, `signal` in the
context, and is given to graphql's `execute` as `abortSignal`, so graphql stops resolving and
rejects the pending work. An open event stream (a subscription) is ended at once by `dispose()`: it
sends `complete`, then the signal aborts, without waiting for `shutdownTimeout` (see
[Subscriptions](./subscriptions.md#cancellation-and-shutdown)).

```ts
const resolvers = {
	Query: {
		report: async (_root, _args, { signal }) => {
			const res = await fetch('https://example.com/slow', { signal });
			return res.text();
		},
	},
};
```

An aborted operation answers `{"errors":[{"message":"The operation was aborted.","extensions":{"code":"OPERATION_ABORTED"}}]}`
with status 499 (the client's request was aborted) or 503 (otherwise: the server is shutting down). It is not an unexpected
failure: `onUnexpected` is not called.

## `getContext()` for code far below a resolver

The resolver's third argument is the way to reach the context. When a helper or a logger is called
deep below a resolver and threading the context through would be noise, `getContext()` is the
shortcut. Inside an operation, `getContext()` returns the same object the resolvers receive, so helpers and
loggers need no extra parameter. It is backed by `AsyncLocalStorage` (`node:async_hooks`).

```ts
import { getContext, tryGetContext } from '@graxia/core';

export function currentUser(): string | undefined {
	return getContext<Ctx>().user?.id;
}

export const log = (message: string) =>
	console.log(tryGetContext<Ctx>()?.user?.id ?? 'no operation', message);
```

- `getContext()` throws a `GraxiaConfigError` outside an operation ("getContext() called outside a graxia operation…").
- `tryGetContext()` returns `undefined` instead.
- `asyncContext: false` on `createGraxia` skips the `AsyncLocalStorage` entirely; `getContext()` then
  throws, its message naming the option. Pass the context explicitly in that case.

The store covers the plugins' `onExecute` hooks and the execution itself, not `onRequest`,
`onParams` or the earlier stages. Prefer the explicit context argument. The cost of the store is measured in
`packages/core/bench/als.ts` (see the pull request that added it).

## `dispose()` and draining

```ts
const graxia = createGraxia({ schema, shutdownTimeout: 5_000 });
const server = graxia.serve({ port: 3000 });

process.on('SIGTERM', async () => {
	await graxia.dispose(); // or: await graxia.dispose({ timeout: 2_000 })
	process.exit(0);
});
```

`dispose(options?)` does, in order:

1. Stops accepting work: a request arriving now answers `503` with
   `{"errors":[{"message":"Server is shutting down.","extensions":{"code":"SHUTTING_DOWN"}}]}` and
   `connection: close`.
2. Calls `server.stop()` (not forced) on every server started with `serve()`.
3. Ends the open event streams at once (each sends `complete`, then its `signal` aborts; see
   [Subscriptions](./subscriptions.md#cancellation-and-shutdown)), then waits for the other in-flight operations to settle, up to `timeout` milliseconds (default
   `shutdownTimeout`, 10 000). Then it aborts their `signal` and waits at most `timeout` more. An
   operation that ignores its signal and is still pending then is reported through `onUnexpected`
   (one error, "dispose: N operation(s) did not settle after abort") and does not block the rest.
4. Waits for the plugins' `setup` to finish, then runs every plugin's `onDispose()` in reverse plugin order. Only the plugins whose `setup` succeeded are
   disposed. Every hook runs even when one throws; the first error is rethrown afterwards.

A second call returns the same promise. `graxia` also implements `Symbol.asyncDispose`:

```ts
{
	await using graxia = createGraxia({ schema });
	// …
} // dispose() runs here
```

A plugin releases what its `setup` opened:

```ts
const db = definePlugin({
	name: 'db',
	setup: async () => {
		await pool.connect();
	},
	onDispose: async () => {
		await pool.end();
	},
});
```

# @graxia/core — Errors

Source: packages/core/docs/guide/errors.md

# Errors

A client sees two kinds of errors. **Exposed** errors are the ones you chose to show: their message,
`extensions.code` and `extensions.fix` reach the response. Everything else is **masked**: the client
gets `Unexpected error.` and a correlation id, and you get the original error through `onUnexpected`.
Masking is always on, in every environment.

## Exposed errors

```ts
import { exposedError } from '@graxia/core';

const resolvers = {
	Query: {
		book: (_parent, { id }, { books }) => {
			const book = books.get(id);
			if (!book)
				throw exposedError('NOT_FOUND', 'Book not found.', {
					fix: 'Check the id.',
					extensions: { id },
				});
			return book;
		},
	},
};
```

The response error is `{ message: "Book not found.", path, locations, extensions: { id, code: "NOT_FOUND", fix: "Check the id." } }`.
Every error graxia itself emits carries one too (see [The `fix` contract](#the-fix-contract)). `fix` is one short sentence telling the client how to recover; `extensions` carries anything else
(`code` and `fix` win over the same names). `isGraxiaError(value)` tells an error made by
`exposedError` from any other value.

What is exposed as is, and what is masked:

| what the resolver threw, or what failed                                 | the client gets                                              |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `exposedError(...)`                                                     | message, `code`, `fix`, `extensions`                         |
| a `GraphQLError` of your own (see the trap below)                       | message and extensions, as is                                |
| graphql's own errors: validation, variable coercion, non-null violation | unchanged                                                    |
| a plain `Error`, a thrown string, a library error                       | `Unexpected error.`, `INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR`, correlation id |

The rule, exactly: an error is **exposed** when it has no `originalError` (graphql's own: validation,
coercion), when it is a genuine non-null violation, or when its original is a `GraphQLError` of any
origin (`exposedError` included). Everything else (a plain `Error`, a thrown string, a library error)
is **masked**. `path` and `locations` are always kept. `originalError` and stacks are never serialized.

## Validation errors

A document that parses but does not validate against the schema answers with graphql's own
errors (exposed), each carrying `extensions.code: "GRAPHQL_VALIDATION_FAILED"` (Apollo
compatible). The HTTP status is unchanged (400 with `application/graphql-response+json`, 200 with
`application/json`). Errors that a plugin supplies with `setResult` keep what the plugin gave them.

## Variable and operation-name errors

A variable that is missing or has the wrong type is refused by graphql before any field runs: the
answer has graphql's message, `extensions.code: "BAD_USER_INPUT"` and a `fix`. An error that
already has a code (an `exposedError` thrown by a custom scalar) keeps it. An operation name the
document does not have, or a missing one when the document holds several operations, is refused by
graxia with the same code and a `fix` that says to send `operationName`.

## Typed codes

`code` is typed as a key of `GraxiaErrorCodes`: `BAD_USER_INPUT`, `UNAUTHENTICATED`, `FORBIDDEN`,
`NOT_FOUND`, `CONFLICT`, `INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR`, and the codes core itself emits
(`GRAPHQL_PARSE_FAILED`, `GRAPHQL_VALIDATION_FAILED`, `OPERATION_ABORTED`, `SHUTTING_DOWN`,
`SUBSCRIPTION_NOT_SUPPORTED`, `INCREMENTAL_NOT_SUPPORTED`). A code that is not in the list fails to
compile. Add your own by augmenting the interface:

```ts
// graxia.d.ts
declare module '@graxia/core' {
	interface GraxiaErrorCodes {
		PAYMENT_REQUIRED: true;
	}
}

exposedError('PAYMENT_REQUIRED', 'Your plan has ended.', {
	fix: 'Renew it in the billing page.',
});
```

## Correlation id

The correlation id is the request id: the `x-request-id` header graxia generates (a client's own
header is never trusted). A masked error and the generic 500 both carry it:

```json
{
	"errors": [
		{
			"message": "Unexpected error.",
			"path": ["book"],
			"extensions": {
				"code": "INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR",
				"correlationId": "5c1b…"
			}
		}
	]
}
```

A user who reports the id lets you find the original error in your logs (see
[troubleshooting](../troubleshooting.md#unexpected-error)).

## `onUnexpected`

`onUnexpected(error, { requestId, correlationId, phase })` receives the original, unmasked error of
every unexpected failure. `requestId` and `correlationId` are the same value; `phase` is `request`
(transport and `onRequest`-level failures), `execution` (a hook, `context` or `execute` failing inside an operation, or a resolver that threw) or
`dispose` (operations left after shutdown, which have no id) or `setup` (a plugin's `setup`
failed; reported once, with no id; see [Plugins](./plugins.md#setup-and-dispose)).

```ts
createGraxia({
	schema,
	onUnexpected: (error, { correlationId, phase }) =>
		logger.error({ err: error, correlationId, phase }),
});
```

By default it logs with `console.error` outside production; in production nothing is logged until you
set it. `false` silences it. An exception thrown by the reporter is swallowed.

## `maskError`

`maskError` replaces the default masker, for the last row of the table only (the unexpected errors).
It receives the error graphql built (with `path`, `nodes`) and the correlation id, and returns the
`GraphQLError` the client gets. The original is still reported through `onUnexpected`.

```ts
import { GraphQLError } from 'graphql';

createGraxia({
	schema,
	maskError: (error, { correlationId }) =>
		new GraphQLError('Something went wrong.', {
			path: error.path ?? [],
			extensions: { code: 'INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR', reference: correlationId },
		}),
});
```

`maskErrors: false` turns masking off: every resolver error reaches the client with its message.
It is unsafe and meant for tests only.

A `maskError` that throws is replaced by the default masker for that error: the client still gets a
masked error, and both the original and the masker's own error reach `onUnexpected`.

## The `GraphQLError` trap

A plain `GraphQLError` thrown from a resolver is **exposed**, not masked (this matches GraphQL Yoga
and eases migration). A library that throws `GraphQLError` with internal details would therefore
leak them. Throw `exposedError` for errors you mean to show, and never put secrets in the message of
a `GraphQLError`. If a dependency throws `GraphQLError` you cannot trust, catch it and rethrow.

Any `GraphQLError` is exposed by design, including one that comes from an upstream client or a
gateway you call: its message and extensions reach your clients. Catch and rethrow such errors as
`exposedError` (or let a plain `Error` be masked).

## Known behaviour: scalar coercion

graphql itself reports a custom scalar's `parseValue` or `parseLiteral` that throws a plain `Error`
as a coercion error with that message, before any resolver runs. Graxia does not mask it (it has no
`originalError` it can tell from a client's mistake). From a scalar, throw
`exposedError('BAD_USER_INPUT', 'Invalid date.')` or a `GraphQLError` with a safe message, never a
message that names internals.

## The `fix` contract

Every error graxia itself emits carries `extensions.fix`, one short sentence saying what the client
changes, in development and in production. Messages and codes do not depend on it.

| the error                                                                                                       | the `fix` says                                                                |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| a syntax error, a document over the token or depth limit                                                        | correct the document at the position the error points to                      |
| a validation failure (unknown field, a limit, introspection off)                                                | change the operation to match the schema                                      |
| a variable that is missing or invalid (`BAD_USER_INPUT`, raised before any field)                               | check the operation against the schema                                        |
| an unknown or missing operation name (`BAD_USER_INPUT`)                                                         | send `operationName`, naming one operation of the document                    |
| an HTTP refusal: 404, 405, 406, 413, 415, invalid JSON or parameters, a batch over its limit, CSRF and `Origin` | what to send instead (a header, a smaller body, one operation)                |
| a subscription over plain JSON, `@defer` or `@stream` over a transport that cannot stream                       | which transport or `Accept` to use, or to remove the directive                |
| trusted documents and APQ refusals, a rate limit, a field selected twice, a shutdown, an aborted operation      | the id or hash to send, when to retry, what to remove                         |
| a null in a non-null field                                                                                      | report it with the request id (a server bug)                                  |
| a masked unexpected error (`INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR`)                                                             | "Retry later; quote the correlationId when you report it." It never says why. |

What graxia never touches: an error you throw. An `exposedError` carries the `fix` you give it (write one, so an
agent can recover), and a `GraphQLError` of your own, including one a `subscribe` threw or an error in a deferred
payload, stays as you wrote it. A validation rule's own `code` and extensions are kept; only a missing `fix` is
added. Errors of a plugin's own executor (a replaced `executeFn`) are the plugin's. See
[Ready for agents](./agent.md) for how an agent reads them, and `lintDescriptions` for the `@errors` codes.

# @graxia/core — GraphQL over HTTP

Source: packages/core/docs/guide/http.md

# GraphQL over HTTP

`createGraxia` serves a schema over [GraphQL over HTTP](https://graphql.github.io/graphql-over-http/)
on Bun. It passes every MUST and SHOULD of the `graphql-http` server audits (61 audits, run against
a real `Bun.serve` in this package's specs).

```ts
import { createGraxia, createSchema } from '@graxia/core';

const schema = createSchema()({
	typeDefs: 'type Query { hello: String }',
	resolvers: { Query: { hello: () => 'world' } },
});

const graxia = createGraxia({ schema });
graxia.serve({ port: 3000 }); // POST/GET http://localhost:3000/graphql
```

`graxia.ready` is a promise that resolves once every plugin's `setup` ran and rejects with the
error of the first one that failed; `await graxia.ready` at startup to fail fast (see
[Plugins](./plugins.md#setup-and-dispose)).

## Options

| option             | default                                           | what it does                                                                                                                                                                 |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `schema`           | required                                          | any `GraphQLSchema` (`createSchema` output included)                                                                                                                         |
| `path`             | `/graphql`                                        | the path served; other paths answer 404. `false` serves any path (your host routes)                                                                                          |
| `context`          | none                                              | `({ request, serverContext, params, signal }) => object`, merged over `serverContext`, then `onContext` plugins run                                                          |
| `plugins`          | `[]`                                              | see [Plugins](./plugins.md)                                                                                                                                                  |
| `limits`           | `tokens` 15000, `nesting` 1000, `bodyBytes` 1 MiB | document limits and body size, plus the operation limits `depth` 12, `aliases` 30, `directives` 50, `rootFields` 20 and `cost` (5 000), see [Limits](./limits-and-caches.md) |
| `caches`           | on                                                | parse and validation caches, or `false`                                                                                                                                      |
| `batching`         | `false`                                           | `false`, or `{ limit: n }`                                                                                                                                                   |
| `csrf`             | on                                                | CSRF header and `Origin` checks, `false` to turn off, see [Security](./security.md)                                                                                          |
| `trustedDocuments` | absent                                            | manifest, `documentId` and APQ, see [Trusted documents](./trusted-documents.md)                                                                                              |
| `telemetry`        | on when `@softistx/telemetry` is installed        | spans on `@softistx/telemetry`, or `false`, see [Telemetry](./telemetry.md)                                                                                                  |
| `introspection`    | `true`, `false` in production                     | answers `__schema` and `__type`                                                                                                                                              |
| `suggestions`      | `true`, `false` in production                     | keeps "Did you mean" hints                                                                                                                                                   |
| `asyncContext`     | `true`                                            | `getContext()` through `AsyncLocalStorage`, see [Context](./context.md)                                                                                                      |
| `shutdownTimeout`  | `10000`                                           | milliseconds `dispose()` waits for in-flight operations                                                                                                                      |
| `onUnexpected`     | `console.error` outside production                | `(error, { requestId, correlationId, phase }) => void` called for every unexpected failure, or `false` to stay silent. Its own exceptions are swallowed                      |

The context of an operation is `{ ...serverContext, ...(await context(...)) }`, then the `onContext`
hooks extend it. CORS is not handled: the host owns it. Invalid options (`limits.bodyBytes` or
`batching.limit` not a positive integer, a `path` not starting with `/`) throw a `GraxiaConfigError`
naming the option when `createGraxia` is called.

## `serve` or your own `Bun.serve`

`graxia.serve(options)` is `Bun.serve({ ...options, fetch })`; Bun's `server` is forwarded in the
`serverContext` (`context.server`), for WebSocket upgrades and client addresses. To keep your own server and routes,
mount `graxia.fetch` (it never rejects and returns a plain `Response`):

```ts
const graxia = createGraxia({ schema, path: false });

Bun.serve({
	port: 3000,
	routes: {
		'/health': () => new Response('ok'),
		// pass `server` too when a client may open event streams (subscriptions.md#bun-idle-timeout)
		'/api/graphql': (request, server) =>
			graxia.fetch(request, { tenant: 'acme', server }),
	},
});
```

To serve WebSockets from your own server too, call `graxia.upgrade(request, server)` from `fetch` when `graxia.isUpgrade(request)` and
pass `graxia.websocket` as `websocket` (see [Subscriptions over WebSocket](./websocket.md)); on the
same path, `serve()` does it for you.

The second argument is the `serverContext`, merged into every operation's context. With `path: false`
graxia answers whatever path it is handed.

The host context is typed on the `context` factory, `({ serverContext }: ContextInit<{ db: Db }>) => …`
(do not write `createGraxia<…>`: an explicit type argument turns the schema check off). When the
type has a required key, the `serverContext` of `fetch`, of `graxia.execute` and of `serve`
(`graxia.serve({ serverContext })`) is required too, and leaving it out is a type error; when
every key is optional (or there is no annotation) it stays optional. `serve` adds `server` (Bun's
server) to it. The compiler checks that the context matches your schema's `createSchema<Ctx>` (see
[Context](./context.md#write-the-context-once)).

## Requests

- **CSRF and origin**: before anything else (and before any plugin), a `GET`, or a `POST` that is not
  JSON, needs one of the CSRF headers, otherwise 403 `CSRF_HEADER_REQUIRED`: a non-JSON `POST` without
  it is a 403, not a 415. A browser `Origin` that does not match is 403 `FORBIDDEN_ORIGIN`. See
  [Security](./security.md).
- **POST** needs `Content-Type: application/json` (a charset, if given, must be UTF-8), otherwise 415.
  The body is `{ query, variables?, operationName?, extensions? }`; `null` means absent.
- **GET** reads `query`, `operationName`, and `variables` / `extensions` as URL-encoded JSON. A
  mutation over GET answers 405 with `Allow: POST`, decided right after parsing and before validation.
- **Accept**: `application/graphql-response+json` or `application/json`. A missing header, `*/*` and
  `application/*` answer `application/json`. Anything else answers 406. q-values are honoured (clamped
  to 0..1; an explicit `q=0` excludes a type even when a wildcard would match). Responses carry
  `Vary: Accept`.
- The body is read as a stream and counted: past `limits.bodyBytes` reading stops and the answer is
  413. `Content-Length` is checked first but never trusted alone.
- Other methods answer 405 with `Allow: GET, POST`.
- **Event streams**: an `Accept` that prefers `text/event-stream` (named, never through a wildcard,
  with a q at least that of the JSON types) answers an event stream for any operation; see
  [Subscriptions](./subscriptions.md). Without it, a subscription (`SUBSCRIPTION_NOT_SUPPORTED`) and
  `@defer` / `@stream` (`INCREMENTAL_NOT_SUPPORTED`) are refused with a 400 under
  `application/graphql-response+json` (200 under `application/json`), the code in `extensions.code`.
  A batch with an event-stream `Accept` answers 400.
- **Multipart**: an `Accept` that prefers `multipart/mixed` (named, never through a wildcard) answers
  a `@defer` / `@stream` query as `multipart/mixed; boundary="-"`; any other result stays plain JSON.
  See [`@defer` and `@stream`](./incremental.md). A batch with it answers 400.

## Status codes

| situation                                                                                                      | `application/graphql-response+json`                                                       | `application/json`       |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------ |
| result with `data` (field errors included)                                                                     | 200                                                                                       | 200                      |
| parse or validation error, unknown operation, bad variables                                                    | 400                                                                                       | 200                      |
| missing `query`; malformed JSON; wrong parameter types                                                         | 400                                                                                       | 400                      |
| subscription, `@defer` / `@stream` (without an event-stream or multipart `Accept`)                             | 400                                                                                       | 200                      |
| mutation over GET                                                                                              | 405 (`Allow: POST`)                                                                       | 405                      |
| path / method / `Accept` / `Content-Type` / size                                                               | 404 / 405 / 406 / 415 / 413                                                               | same                     |
| missing CSRF header (`CSRF_HEADER_REQUIRED`), foreign `Origin` (`FORBIDDEN_ORIGIN`)                            | 403                                                                                       | same                     |
| a `fieldRateLimit` limit exceeded (`RATE_LIMITED`, `Retry-After`)                                              | 429                                                                                       | same                     |
| a `single` rate-limited field selected twice (`FIELD_SELECTED_ONCE`)                                           | 400                                                                                       | same                     |
| `PERSISTED_QUERY_ONLY`, `PERSISTED_QUERY_NOT_FOUND` for a `documentId`, a `documentId` sent with a `query`     | 400                                                                                       | same                     |
| APQ hash: `PERSISTED_QUERY_NOT_FOUND`, `_NOT_SUPPORTED`, `_VERSION_NOT_SUPPORTED`, `PROVIDED_SHA_DOESNT_MATCH` | 400                                                                                       | 200 (the retry protocol) |
| client left, or shutdown past its timeout (`OPERATION_ABORTED`)                                                | 499 / 503                                                                                 | same                     |
| `dispose()` started (`SHUTTING_DOWN`)                                                                          | 503 (`connection: close`)                                                                 | same                     |
| plugin hook threw, `context` threw, `execute` threw                                                            | 500 `{ errors: [{ message: "Unexpected error.", extensions: { code, correlationId } }] }` | same                     |

Unexpected failures never leak their message. The body is generic whatever the cause
(`INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR` and a `correlationId` equal to the `x-request-id` header); the original
error reaches `onUnexpected` with that id. A resolver that throws a plain error is masked the same
way inside a normal result (see [Errors](./errors.md)). `fetch` never rejects: a response Bun would refuse
(such as `Response.error()`) also becomes this 500. A throwing executor still runs the `onExecute`
after-hooks, and every after-hook runs exactly once on every path.

## Plugin headers

Every hook payload has `responseHeaders: Headers`. What a plugin sets there is merged into whatever
response ends the request, a 413 or a short-circuit included: `set-cookie` and `vary` are appended,
any other header is set only when the response does not already carry it.

```ts
const noStore = definePlugin({
	name: 'no-store',
	onRequest: ({ responseHeaders }) => {
		responseHeaders.set('cache-control', 'no-store');
	},
});
```

Path and method refusals (404, 405) happen before any plugin runs. Every other response goes through
`onRequest` after-hooks and `onResponse`.

## Batching

Off by default: a JSON array body answers 400. With `batching: { limit: 10 }` an array runs its
entries **one after the other, in order** (a later entry may rely on an earlier mutation, and one
request cannot multiply its own concurrency) and answers 200 with an array of results. More than
`limit` entries, an empty array or a malformed entry answers 400. A hook that throws, or an
executor that throws, in entry _n_ becomes that entry's generic `Unexpected error.` body (with the request's `correlationId`)
in the array and the batch carries on (earlier mutations already ran, later entries still run). A
plugin that short-circuits with `respond` (in `onRequest`, or in an entry's `onParams`) is a decision
about the request and answers the whole request.

Each entry runs on its own forked [state](./plugins.md#per-request-state): writes in one entry are
not seen by the next, reads fall through to what `onRequest` set.

## Request id

Each request gets `crypto.randomUUID()`, kept in the request state and sent
as the `x-request-id` response header, on every response. A client's `x-request-id` is never
trusted nor echoed, so an invalid or hostile header changes nothing. Plugins read the id with
`getRequestId(state)`; they cannot set it.

```ts
import { getRequestId } from '@graxia/core';

const log = definePlugin({
	name: 'log',
	onRequest: ({ state }) => console.log('request', getRequestId(state)),
});
```

# @graxia/core — `@defer` and `@stream`

Source: packages/core/docs/guide/incremental.md

# `@defer` and `@stream`

Incremental delivery sends the parts of a result as they become ready: a query with `@defer` or
`@stream` answers a first payload at once, then more payloads until `hasNext` is `false`. It is on by
default for queries and mutations, over `multipart/mixed` and over server-sent events.

```ts
import { createGraxia, createSchema } from '@graxia/core';

const schema = createSchema()({
	typeDefs:
		'type Query { user: User friends: [String!]! } type User { name: String slow: String }',
	resolvers: {
		/* ... */
	},
});
const graxia = createGraxia({ schema }); // incremental delivery is on
```

`createSchema` adds the `@defer` and `@stream` directives to the schemas it builds (unless your SDL
declares them). A `GraphQLSchema` you build yourself needs them in its directives, or validation
answers `Unknown directive "@defer".`:

```ts
import {
	GraphQLDeferDirective,
	GraphQLSchema,
	GraphQLStreamDirective,
	specifiedDirectives,
} from 'graphql';

new GraphQLSchema({
	query,
	directives: [
		...specifiedDirectives,
		GraphQLDeferDirective,
		GraphQLStreamDirective,
	],
});
```

## Which `Accept` gets what

| `Accept`                                                             | answer                                                     |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `multipart/mixed` (with or without `deferSpec` / `subscriptionSpec`) | `multipart/mixed; boundary="-"`, one JSON part per payload |
| `text/event-stream`                                                  | one `next` event per payload, then `complete`              |
| `application/graphql-response+json`, `application/json`, `*/*`       | refused with `INCREMENTAL_NOT_SUPPORTED` (400 / 200)       |

`multipart/mixed` is chosen only when named (never through a wildcard). For an incremental operation
(`@defer`, `@stream`) it is used whenever it is named with a q above 0, even when a JSON type is listed
first or ranks higher, because clients that list JSON first, such as GraphiQL, send
`Accept: application/json, multipart/mixed`. `text/event-stream` is chosen
only when not ranked below a JSON type. Any other operation keeps the usual negotiation (JSON here). A query that does not turn out incremental, and any error before
execution (parse, validation), is answered as plain JSON even under a `multipart/mixed` `Accept`,
which clients such as Apollo Client read. A batch with either `Accept` answers 400.

The multipart framing is the one of the incremental delivery over HTTP specification: boundary `-`,
each part `\r\n---\r\ncontent-type: application/json; charset=utf-8\r\n\r\n<json>`, the response
ending with `\r\n-----\r\n`. There is no keep-alive part: a query is finite.

## Formats

```ts
createGraxia({ schema, incremental: { format: 'graphql17' } }); // the default
createGraxia({ schema, incremental: { format: 'legacy' } });
```

- `graphql17` is graphql 17's format: the initial result lists `pending` ids, each later payload has
  `incremental` entries and `completed` ids, and `hasNext`. Apollo Client 4 reads it
  (`GraphQL17Alpha9Handler`).
- `legacy` is the 2022-08 format (`incremental` entries with `path` and `label`, no ids), which older
  Apollo, urql and Relay clients read. graxia runs graphql's `legacyExecuteIncrementally`.
- `incremental: false` turns delivery off: an incremental result is released and the query is refused
  with `INCREMENTAL_NOT_SUPPORTED`. The executor is still graphql's `experimentalExecuteIncrementally`
  (graphql's plain `execute` throws for a schema that declares `@defer`); a query without `@defer` or
  `@stream` is answered as usual.

## A client

```ts
// bun add -d meros
import { meros } from 'meros';

const response = await fetch('http://localhost:3000/graphql', {
	method: 'POST',
	headers: {
		'content-type': 'application/json',
		accept: 'multipart/mixed;deferSpec=20220824, application/json',
	},
	body: JSON.stringify({ query: '{ user { name ... @defer { slow } } }' }),
});
const parts = await meros(response);
for await (const part of parts) console.log(part.body);
```

## Running the schema elsewhere

`createSchema` declares `@defer` and `@stream`, and graphql's plain `execute` refuses such a schema
(`The provided schema unexpectedly contains experimental directives (@defer or @stream). These directives may only be utilized if experimental execution features are explicitly enabled.`). Run it through graxia or `experimentalExecuteIncrementally`, or build it without the
directives when it only feeds plain `execute`:

```ts
createSchema()({ typeDefs, resolvers, incremental: false });
```

Such a schema cannot serve incremental queries.

## Hooks, masking, context

- `onResultChunk` runs for every payload, initial and subsequent, before masking; `setChunk` replaces
  it.
- Unexpected resolver errors are masked on every payload: the top-level `errors`, and the `errors` of
  each `incremental` and `completed` entry. The original reaches `onUnexpected` once, with the same
  correlation id.
- `onExecute` runs once, around the executor; its `setExecuteFn` may return graphql's incremental
  results (`{ initialResult, subsequentResults }`).
- `getContext()` works in deferred and streamed resolvers (`asyncContext`).

## Cancellation and shutdown

The stream is pulled one payload at a time. When the client leaves or cancels the body, the
operation's `signal` aborts and graxia calls `subsequentResults.return()`.

Over HTTP (multipart/mixed, SSE), `dispose()` lets an incremental query or mutation drain like any other operation: it keeps streaming
its deferred parts for up to `shutdownTimeout`. A stream still open after that is cut (a multipart
response gets its closing boundary, an event stream gets `complete`) and its resolvers see the
operation's `signal` abort. Only subscriptions end as soon as `dispose()` starts (see
[Subscriptions](./subscriptions.md)). Over WebSocket there is no drain: `dispose()` closes the
socket with 1001 and ends every operation on it.

## Limits

- Not over plain JSON, and not through `graxia.execute` or the test client (they return the
  `INCREMENTAL_NOT_SUPPORTED` error in the result).
- Not inside subscription events: a subscription event that uses `@defer` / `@stream` is refused with
  `INCREMENTAL_NOT_SUPPORTED`.
- Not in a batch.

# @graxia/core — Limits and caches

Source: packages/core/docs/guide/limits-and-caches.md

# Limits and caches

Before a document is parsed, graxia bounds it; once parsed, it keeps the result. Both are
configured on `createGraxia` and apply to every operation, including those of `graxia.execute`
(for a string document).

```ts
createGraxia({
	schema,
	limits: { tokens: 15_000, nesting: 1_000, bodyBytes: 1_048_576 },
	caches: {
		parse: { maxBytes: 64 * 1024 * 1024, max: 1024, ttlMs: 3_600_000 },
		validation: {},
	},
});
```

A failed parse or validation answers the client with `GRAPHQL_PARSE_FAILED` or
`GRAPHQL_VALIDATION_FAILED` errors. The parse limits bound parsing; the
[operation limits](#operation-limits) below bound what an operation asks for.

The `onParse` and `onValidate` plugin stages run around these steps; their after-hooks receive the
outcome and run even when a validation rule throws.

## A key-value cache for your own code

`createMemoryCache` is a small asynchronous key-value store (LRU, per-entry time to live) behind the
`KeyValueCache` contract. The store of automatic persisted queries is one (`trustedDocuments.store`, see
[Trusted documents](./trusted-documents.md)); upcoming features (response caching) take one too,
and your own plugins can use it today. `redisCache` from
`@graxia/redis` implements the same contract across processes.

```ts
import { createMemoryCache } from '@graxia/core';

const cache = createMemoryCache({ maxEntries: 500 });
await cache.set('greeting', 'hello', { ttlMs: 60_000 });
await cache.get('greeting'); // 'hello'
await cache.delete('greeting'); // true
```

Values are strings by default (serialise yourself); `createMemoryCache<V>()` stores any `V`.
`maxEntries` defaults to 1000; an expired entry is dropped when read.

## Parse limits

| Option           | Default | Meaning                                                           |
| ---------------- | ------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `limits.tokens`  | 15 000  | Most tokens (graphql 17 `parse(source, { maxTokens })`)           |
| `limits.nesting` | 1 000   | Most `{`, `(`, `[` levels, counted on the raw source before parse |

`false` turns a limit off. Strings, block strings and comments are not counted for nesting.
Every failure is a `GraphQLError` with `extensions.code = 'GRAPHQL_PARSE_FAILED'`; the token
and nesting cases add `extensions.limit` and `extensions.fix`. A parser stack overflow
(`RangeError`, a document nested just under `limits.nesting` that still overflows the parser) is
reported the same way, never thrown and never masked as `Unexpected error.`; it carries `fix` but
no `limit`, and is not cached.

## Operation limits

On by default, so an operation over them is refused before it executes. Each is a positive
integer, or `false` to turn it off; anything else throws a `GraxiaConfigError` when
`createGraxia` runs.

| Option                        | Default | Constant                  | Counts                                                           |
| ----------------------------- | ------- | ------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `limits.depth`                | 12      | `DEFAULT_MAX_DEPTH`       | The deepest field selection; root fields are depth 1             |
| `limits.aliases`              | 30      | `DEFAULT_MAX_ALIASES`     | Aliased fields                                                   |
| `limits.directives`           | 50      | `DEFAULT_MAX_DIRECTIVES`  | Directive usages                                                 |
| `limits.rootFields`           | 20      | `DEFAULT_MAX_ROOT_FIELDS` | Fields of the operation's root selection (`__typename` excluded) |
| `limits.cost.max`             | 5 000   | `DEFAULT_MAX_COST`        | The [cost](#cost) of the operation (`cost: false` turns it off)  |
| `limits.cost.defaultListSize` | 10      | `DEFAULT_LIST_SIZE`       | Items assumed in a list with no size information                 |
| `limits.cost.objectCost`      | 1       |                           | Cost of an object with no `@cost`                                |
| `limits.cost.scalarCost`      | 0       |                           | Cost of a scalar or enum with no `@cost`                         |

All four count through fragments and inline fragments: a fragment spread twice counts twice.
The walk is memoised per fragment, so a document of fragments that each spread the previous
one twice stays linear, and a fragment cycle (reported by validation) cannot hang it.
`__typename` adds no depth. An introspection root (`__schema`, `__type`) is a field, an alias and
directives like any other, and costs `objectCost`; only the depth of its subtree is exempt, so
GraphiQL's introspection query passes the defaults while 200 aliased `__schema` roots do not.
`@skip` and `@include` are ignored by the limits (a skipped field still counts: an over-estimate).
The limits are validation rules added to graphql's: a plugin whose `onValidate` replaces the
validation function (`setValidationFn`) may drop them.

A refusal is a `GRAPHQL_VALIDATION_FAILED` error (HTTP 400, an `error` message over WebSocket,
`next` then `complete` over server-sent events), one per limit exceeded, with `extensions.limit`
(`{ name, max, actual }`) and `extensions.fix`:

```json
{
	"message": "Operation depth 14 exceeds the limit of 12.",
	"extensions": {
		"code": "GRAPHQL_VALIDATION_FAILED",
		"limit": { "name": "depth", "max": 12, "actual": 14 },
		"fix": "Ask for fewer nested fields or raise limits.depth."
	}
}
```

Size them from your own clients' largest legitimate operation, plus headroom: log the
`actual` of refusals while you tune.

```ts
createGraxia({
	schema,
	limits: { depth: 8, aliases: 10, directives: false, rootFields: 10 },
});
```

depth, aliases, directives and rootFields are validation rules, so the validation cache still
serves them (the limits are fixed per instance). A plugin's `onValidate` rules keep working.

### Reading the limits in force

`graxia.limits` holds the resolved `bodyBytes` and `tokens` (`tokens` is `false` when that limit is
off), and `graxia.schema` the schema served. A layer in front of the instance, such as
`@graxia/mcp`, reads them to enforce the same numbers instead of asking you to repeat them.

### Cost

The cost follows the `@cost` and `@listSize` directives (the IBM GraphQL cost directive
design, as Apollo and Hot Chocolate read them). `createSchema` adds their definitions unless your
SDL declares them; for a `GraphQLSchema` you build yourself, add `costDirectives`. A schema
without the directives still gets the default costs.

```graphql
type Query {
	users(first: Int): [User!]!
		@listSize(slicingArguments: ["first"], assumedSize: 20)
	report: Report @cost(weight: 50)
	orders(first: Int): OrderConnection
		@listSize(slicingArguments: ["first"], sizedFields: ["edges"])
}
```

```ts
createGraxia({
	schema,
	limits: {
		cost: { max: 5_000, defaultListSize: 10, objectCost: 1, scalarCost: 0 },
	},
});
```

- A field costs its own `@cost` weight, else its return type's `@cost` weight, else
  `objectCost` (object, interface, union) or `scalarCost` (scalar, enum).
- A list field multiplies its items by the list size: the largest value of its slicing
  arguments (`slicingArguments`, a name or a dotted path into an input such as `page.size`), else
  `assumedSize`, else `defaultListSize`. A weight written on the field itself is paid once; one from
  the type or the defaults is paid per item. `sizedFields` gives the connection's list fields (`edges`,
  `nodes`) that size instead.
- The slicing arguments read the request's coerced variable values (defaults included), so
  `first: $n` cannot get around the limit. That is why cost is checked per request, after validation
  and before execution, on every transport, rather than as a validation rule.
- `requireOneSlicingArgument` (true by default) is enforced: a list field whose slicing arguments
  are all absent, `null`, negative, not an integer or an unprovided variable is refused with
  `Field Query.users requires one of its slicing arguments (first, last).`, instead of falling back to
  a default size. Set it to `false` on the `@listSize` to allow the fallback. A huge value
  (`first: 2147483647`) is just a big cost, refused by `max`.
- A nested list (`[[User!]!]!`) multiplies per level; the inner levels use `assumedSize`, else
  `defaultListSize`.
- Variables that do not coerce are not costed: execution reports them as usual.
- `@defer` and `@stream` cost the full operation. Introspection roots cost `objectCost` each. Cost
  is a conservative upper bound: fields in every branch of an abstract type are summed, and
  `@skip` / `@include` are ignored.
- `@cost` and `@listSize` are read from the SDL (the `astNode` of the field and type), so a
  schema built in code without SDL gets the default costs only. `@cost` on an argument or an input
