```ts
		scopes: { read: 'mcp:read', write: 'mcp:write' }, // default
		resourceName: 'Library', // shown by the metadata
		documentation: 'https://docs.example.com/mcp', // `resource_documentation`
		verifyToken: async (token, request) => verify(token), // McpAuthInfo | Response | undefined
		audience: 'resource', // default: the info's audience must contain `resource`
	},
	mutations: true, // list graphql_mutate and the mutation typed tools, default false
	operations: {
		// persisted operations as typed tools: see the operations guide
		documents: manifest, // core's TrustedManifest: codegen or Relay object, Apollo manifest, Map
		include: (operation) => operation.kind === 'query', // { name, kind, id } => boolean
		descriptions: { BookById: 'Find a book by its id.' }, // by operation name; wins over the document's
	},
	genericTools: false, // only graphql_schema and the typed tools, default true
	allowedOrigins: ['https://app.example'], // browser origins: CORS and the origin check
	allowedHosts: ['mcp.example.com'], // hostnames of the endpoint, default localhost
	onError: (error) => logger.error(error), // default console.error
});
```

## Typed tools

```ts
import { createGraxia } from '@graxia/core';
import { createMcp } from '@graxia/mcp';
import manifest from './persisted-documents.json';

// In the manifest: """Find a book by its id.""" query BookById($id: ID!) { book(id: $id) { id title } }
const graxia = createGraxia({ schema, trustedDocuments: { manifest } });
const mcp = createMcp(graxia, {
	name: 'library',
	operations: { documents: manifest },
});
```

Each named query of the manifest is a tool (`BookById` → `book_by_id`; mutations with
`mutations: true`; subscriptions are skipped) whose input schema comes from the operation's
variables (types, defaults, `@constraint`) and whose output schema comes from its selection set. The
agent sends arguments, not GraphQL. With trusted documents in `strict` mode these are the only tools
that run operations: `graphql_query` and `graphql_mutate` are not listed and refuse a call. Every
operation needs a description (`"""…"""` above it, or `descriptions`); `createMcp` throws one error
listing every problem of the manifest, each with its fix. See
[the operations guide](./docs/guide/operations.md).

## OAuth

```ts
import { createGraxia } from '@graxia/core';
import { createMcp, mcpAuth } from '@graxia/mcp';

// `schema` is the one from the core quick start. `verifyJwt` is your token check (signature and
// issuer): it resolves the claims, and must resolve undefined for a bad token, not throw
// (a throw is an outage: a 503 the client retries).
const graxia = createGraxia({
	schema,
	context: () => ({ userId: mcpAuth()?.subject }), // the verified token, in a tool call
});
const mcp = createMcp(graxia, {
	name: 'library',
	mutations: true,
	auth: {
		resource: 'https://api.example.com/mcp', // the public URL of the endpoint
		authorizationServers: ['https://auth.example.com'],
		verifyToken: async (token) => {
			const claims = await verifyJwt(token);
			if (!claims) return undefined; // a 401
			return {
				subject: claims.sub,
				scopes: claims.scope.split(' '),
				expiresAt: claims.exp, // seconds
				audience: claims.aud, // must contain `resource`
			};
		},
	},
});

Bun.serve({
	routes: {
		[mcp.metadataPath]: mcp.metadata, // RFC 9728 metadata
		'/mcp': (request, server) => mcp.fetch(request, { server }),
	},
	fetch: graxia.fetch,
});
```

A request without a valid bearer token with `mcp:read` is a 401 with a `WWW-Authenticate`
challenge pointing at the metadata; `graphql_mutate` and the mutation typed tools need `mcp:write`. The token's audience is
checked against `resource` unless `audience: 'verifier'` says your verifier did it; a verifier
that throws is a 503, and it may resolve its own `Response`. Bearer only, no DPoP. See
[the auth guide](./docs/guide/auth.md).

## Documentation

See [`docs/`](./docs): [getting started](./docs/guide/getting-started.md), [auth](./docs/guide/auth.md), [tools](./docs/guide/tools.md),
[typed tools](./docs/guide/operations.md),
[security](./docs/guide/security.md), [troubleshooting](./docs/troubleshooting.md)
([auth errors](./docs/troubleshooting-auth.md)) and the
[roadmap](./docs/roadmap.md). The schema and the body limit come from the graxia instance
(`graxia.schema`, `graxia.limits`, core 0.5).

# @graxia/mcp — OAuth resource server

Source: packages/mcp/docs/guide/auth.md

# OAuth resource server

With `auth`, `@graxia/mcp` is an OAuth 2.1 **resource server** (MCP authorization spec, RFC 9728,
RFC 8707): it accepts bearer access tokens, it never issues them. Your authorization server does.

## The flow

1. The client calls `/mcp` with no token: **401** and
   `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="https://api.example.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp", scope="mcp:read"`.
2. It reads that metadata (`mcp.metadata`) and signs the user in at the authorization server it
   names, asking for a token for this resource.
3. It retries with `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.

## Mount it

```ts
import { createGraxia } from '@graxia/core';
import { createMcp } from '@graxia/mcp';

const graxia = createGraxia({ schema });
const mcp = createMcp(graxia, {
	name: 'library',
	mutations: true,
	auth: {
		resource: 'https://api.example.com/mcp',
		authorizationServers: ['https://auth.example.com'],
		verifyToken: async (token) => {
			// your verifier (signature, issuer): it resolves undefined for a bad token, see below
			const claims = await verifyJwt(token);
			if (!claims) return undefined; // a 401
			return {
				subject: claims.sub,
				clientId: claims.client_id,
				scopes: claims.scope.split(' '),
				expiresAt: claims.exp, // seconds
				audience: claims.aud, // compared with `resource`
			};
		},
	},
});

Bun.serve({
	routes: {
		[mcp.metadataPath]: mcp.metadata, // /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp
		'/mcp': (request, server) => mcp.fetch(request, { server }),
	},
	fetch: graxia.fetch,
});
```

`metadataPath` is the RFC 9728 well-known path with the path of `resource` inserted. It is typed
`string` when `auth` is passed to `createMcp`, and is `undefined` without it. `metadata` answers GET
with the JSON document (CORS `*`, `Cache-Control: max-age=3600`), any other method with a 405, and
a 404 without `auth`. `scopes_supported` lists the write scope only with `mutations: true`.

## Options

| option                 | meaning                                                                          |
| ---------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `resource`             | canonical URL of the endpoint, what tokens are issued for; no query, no fragment |
| `authorizationServers` | issuer URLs (absolute, at least one), published in the metadata                  |
| `verifyToken`          | `(token, request) => McpAuthInfo \| Response \| undefined`, see below            |
| `audience`             | `'resource'` (default) or `'verifier'`: who checks the audience, see below       |
| `scopes`               | `{ read, write }`, default `mcp:read` and `mcp:write`                            |
| `resourceName`         | `resource_name` of the metadata                                                  |
| `documentation`        | `resource_documentation` of the metadata                                         |

A wrong `resource` or `authorizationServers` throws at `createMcp`
([troubleshooting auth](../troubleshooting-auth.md)).

## `verifyToken`

It receives the token of `Authorization: Bearer <token>` and the request. It must read the
request's headers only, **never its body**: the body is read after the gate.

It resolves the token's `McpAuthInfo`, `undefined` for a token it does not accept, or a `Response`
when it builds its own refusals: that response is sent as is (plus the CORS headers of an allowed
origin). A **throw is an outage, not a bad token**: the client gets a 503 with `Retry-After: 5`
and the error goes to `onError`.

**Do not let a bad token throw.** Many JWT libraries reject an expired, badly signed or
wrong-audience token by throwing (jose's `jwtVerify` does). Passed through, every expired token
becomes a 503 the client retries for ever instead of a 401 it refreshes on, and each one reaches
`onError`. Catch the library's invalid-token errors and resolve `undefined`; let only real outages
(a JWKS fetch, an introspection call) throw:

```ts
verifyToken: async (token) => {
	let claims;
	try {
		claims = await verifyJwt(token); // throws InvalidTokenError, or a network error
	} catch (error) {
		if (error instanceof InvalidTokenError) return undefined; // a bad token: 401
		throw error; // an outage: 503, retried
	}
	return { subject: claims.sub, scopes: claims.scope.split(' '), audience: claims.aud };
},
```

Tell the two apart by the error's class, as above. With jose (`import { errors } from 'jose'`),
`errors.JWTExpired`, `JWTClaimValidationFailed`, `JWSSignatureVerificationFailed`, `JWTInvalid`,
`JWSInvalid`, `JWKSNoMatchingKey` and `JOSEAlgNotAllowed` are bad tokens; `JWKSTimeout` and a failed
fetch are outages. A bare `catch { return undefined }` would
hide an outage as a 401 and make clients sign in again for nothing.

`McpAuthInfo` is `{ subject?, clientId?, scopes, expiresAt?, audience?, extra? }`:

- `scopes` is required, an array (empty for none).
- `expiresAt` is optional and **in seconds** since the epoch (the `exp` claim). A value in
  milliseconds, `NaN` or `Infinity` is refused.
- `audience` is the `aud` claim, a string or a list.

Only the `Bearer` scheme is read. **DPoP is not supported**: `Authorization: DPoP <token>` gets the
401 of a missing token.

## What is checked, in order

After the origin, host and method checks, and before the body is read:

| case                                          | answer                                                      |
| --------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `access_token` in the query string            | 400, `MCP_TOKEN_IN_URL` (OAuth 2.1 forbids it)              |
| no `Authorization: Bearer`                    | 401, `MCP_UNAUTHORIZED`, challenge with `scope="mcp:read"`  |
| `verifyToken` throws                          | 503, `Retry-After: 5`, `onError`                            |
| it resolves a `Response`                      | that response                                               |
| it resolves `undefined`                       | 401, `error="invalid_token"`                                |
| no `scopes` array, or an unusable `expiresAt` | 401, `invalid_token`, and `onError` (a verifier bug)        |
| `expiresAt` in the past                       | 401, `invalid_token`                                        |
| no `audience`, or one without `resource`      | 401, `invalid_token` (unless `audience: 'verifier'`)        |
| token without the read scope                  | 403, `error="insufficient_scope"`, `MCP_INSUFFICIENT_SCOPE` |

Every refusal of graxia's is a JSON-RPC error with a `fix`. A preflight from an allowed origin
needs no token, and `WWW-Authenticate` is exposed to allowed origins.

## Audience

A token issued for another service must never be accepted here, so the check is on by default:
`verifyToken` returns `audience`, and it must contain `resource` (a fragment and one trailing slash
are ignored). A token whose info has **no** `audience` is refused.

When your verifier already refuses tokens issued for another resource (an introspection endpoint
bound to this resource, a library that takes the resource as an option), say so:

```ts
auth: { resource, authorizationServers, verifyToken, audience: 'verifier' },
```

Nothing is compared then, and a returned `audience` is only handed to `can` and `mcpAuth()`.

## Scopes and step-up

The read scope opens every tool but the ones that write: `graphql_mutate` and the
[typed tools](./operations.md) of mutations. Those are listed only when `mutations: true` **and**
the token has the write scope; a read-only token also gets an overview without the `Mutation`
root. A read-only token that calls one anyway (a stale tool list), alone or inside a JSON-RPC
batch, gets a **403** `error="insufficient_scope", scope="mcp:read mcp:write"` whose description
names the tool called (`rename_book needs the scope mcp:write`): the step-up challenge that tells
the client to re-authorize with both scopes. It is an HTTP answer, not a tool error (the SDK's
tool `scopeChallenge` cannot guard a tool that is not registered for that caller).

With `mutations` off there is no step-up, since no scope opens these tools: the call gets the
protocol's `Tool graphql_mutate not found` (`Tool rename_book not found`). A mutation tool that
`can` hides from the caller gets no step-up either: it answers like a tool that does not exist.

## The principal

`can(request, serverContext, auth)` receives the verified `McpAuthInfo` as its third argument, so
the schema a caller sees can follow its scopes or roles.

`mcpAuth()` returns the same info anywhere during a tool call, for graxia's `context` builder and
resolvers, with no second verification. Outside a tool call, and during a call to an instance
without `auth`, it is `undefined`.

```ts
import { mcpAuth } from '@graxia/mcp';

const graxia = createGraxia({
	schema,
	context: () => ({ userId: mcpAuth()?.subject }),
});
```

The `Authorization` header is still forwarded to `graxia.execute`, so a context builder that
verifies tokens itself keeps working.

## With `@softistx/janus-oauth`

`bearerCaller` resolves a request to its caller (an API key or an access token for the resource)
or to the `Response` to answer instead, so it is the whole verifier. No dependency is added to
`@graxia/mcp`.

```ts
import {
	type BearerCaller,
	bearerCaller,
	protectedResource,
} from '@softistx/janus-oauth';
import { createMcp, mcpAuth } from '@graxia/mcp';

const resource = 'https://api.example.com/mcp';
const issuer = 'https://auth.example.com';
// `accounts` is your janus() instance, `oauth` your authorization server.
const callerOf = bearerCaller({
	accounts,
	oauth,
	resource: protectedResource({
		resource,
		issuer,
		scopes: ['mcp:read', 'mcp:write'],
	}),
});

const mcp = createMcp(graxia, {
	name: 'library',
	mutations: true,
	auth: {
		resource,
		authorizationServers: [issuer],
		audience: 'verifier', // bearerCaller refuses a token for another resource
		verifyToken: async (_token, request) => {
			const caller = await callerOf(request);
			return caller instanceof Response
				? caller
				: { subject: caller.userId, scopes: caller.scopes, extra: { caller } };
		},
	},
});

// In graxia's context builder: what the key or the grant is pinned to.
const context = () => {
	const caller = mcpAuth()?.extra?.['caller'] as BearerCaller | undefined;
	return {
		userId: caller?.userId,
		bound: caller?.bound ?? null,
		authorizationDetails: caller?.authorizationDetails ?? [],
	};
};
```

- `protectedResource({ resource, scopes })` must use the **same URL** as `auth.resource`, and list
  the read and the write scope (`mcp:read`, `mcp:write`, or your `auth.scopes`): an unscoped API
  key holds exactly those.
- `bearerCaller`'s refusals (401 with its challenge, 503 on a store outage) are returned as they
  are. It checks the expiry and the audience itself, hence no `expiresAt` and `audience: 'verifier'`.
- `verifyToken` must not read the request body: hand the request to `callerOf` untouched, it
  authenticates from the headers.
- A DPoP-bound token is not accepted by `@graxia/mcp`; leave `dpop` off on `protectedResource`.

# @graxia/mcp — Getting started

Source: packages/mcp/docs/guide/getting-started.md

# Getting started

## Install and mount

```sh
bun add @graxia/mcp @graxia/core graphql
```

```ts
import { createGraxia } from '@graxia/core';
import { createMcp } from '@graxia/mcp';

// `schema` is the one from the core quick start
const graxia = createGraxia({ schema });
const mcp = createMcp(graxia, { name: 'library' });

Bun.serve({
	routes: { '/mcp': (request, server) => mcp.fetch(request, { server }) },
	fetch: graxia.fetch,
});
```

`createMcp(graxia, options)` reads the schema and the body limit from the instance
(`graxia.schema`, `graxia.limits.bodyBytes`, `@graxia/core` 0.5), so nothing is given twice. `mcp.fetch(request, serverContext?)` is a Web `Request` in, a
`Response` out, and never rejects. `mcp.dispose()` stops the handler (in-flight requests are aborted),
like `graxia.dispose()`.

**In production.** graxia runs trusted documents in `strict` mode there (`NODE_ENV=production`), so
agents cannot run a document they write: pass `operations: { documents }` to give them your
persisted operations as tools ([typed tools](./operations.md)), or `createMcp` reports it through
`onError` at boot. A hand-made host (a test double) must pass `trustedDocuments:
graxia.trustedDocuments` along with `execute`, `schema` and `limits`.

## Transport

Streamable HTTP, stateless: every `POST` carries one JSON-RPC message or a batch of them and is answered on its own.
There is no `Mcp-Session-Id`. `GET` (the optional server-to-client stream) and `DELETE` (closing a
session) answer 405 with a `fix`, as the spec allows. Only `application/json` bodies are accepted.

## Connect a client

Claude Code:

```sh
claude mcp add --transport http library http://localhost:3000/mcp
```

With `auth` set, give the client its token (`--header "Authorization: Bearer <token>"`) or let its
OAuth support follow the 401 to the metadata ([auth](./auth.md)). Any other client takes the URL as a Streamable HTTP server. In a test, use
`@modelcontextprotocol/client` (`Client` and `StreamableHTTPClientTransport`) against `Bun.serve({ port: 0 })`.

## Host context

`serverContext` is the second argument of `mcp.fetch`, typed like `graxia.fetch`'s (it is required
when your host context has required keys, see core's [context guide](https://github.com/softistx/graxia/blob/develop/packages/core/docs/guide/context.md)). Graxia
merges it into the context of every operation, and `can` receives it:

```ts
Bun.serve({
	routes: {
		'/mcp': (request, server) =>
			mcp.fetch(request, { server, tenant: tenantOf(request) }),
	},
	fetch: (request, server) =>
		graxia.fetch(request, { server, tenant: tenantOf(request) }),
});
```

The request's own headers (an `Authorization`, a cookie) are forwarded to `graxia.execute` too, minus
`Content-Type`, `Content-Length`, `Accept`, `Host`, `Origin` and the `Mcp-*` headers (the
serverContext never travels in a header: a client cannot forge it), so a `context`
that reads them works the same over MCP and HTTP.

## Typed tools

To give agents your persisted operations as tools with typed arguments, see
[persisted operations as typed tools](./operations.md).

## Server instructions

`instructions` is shown to the model when it connects: say what the API is for in two or three
sentences. The tools already tell it to call `graphql_schema` first.

# @graxia/mcp — Persisted operations as typed tools

Source: packages/mcp/docs/guide/operations.md

# Persisted operations as typed tools

Give `createMcp` the operations your clients already persist and each one becomes an MCP tool: a
name, a description, a JSON Schema for its arguments (from the operation's variables) and one for
its result (from its selection set). An agent calls `book_by_id({ id: "1" })` instead of writing
GraphQL, and runs only operations you have reviewed.

```ts
import { createGraxia } from '@graxia/core';
import { createMcp } from '@graxia/mcp';
import manifest from './persisted-documents.json';

const graxia = createGraxia({ schema, trustedDocuments: { manifest } });
const mcp = createMcp(graxia, {
	name: 'library',
	operations: { documents: manifest },
});
```

That is all: no handler to write. With this operation in the manifest

```graphql
"""
Find a book by its id.
"""
query BookById(
	"""
	The book id.
	"""
	$id: ID!
) {
	book(id: $id) {
		id
		title
	}
}
```

`tools/list` holds

```json
{
	"name": "book_by_id",
	"title": "BookById",
	"description": "Find a book by its id.",
	"inputSchema": {
		"type": "object",
		"properties": { "id": { "type": "string", "description": "The book id." } },
		"required": ["id"],
		"additionalProperties": false
	},
	"annotations": { "readOnlyHint": true }
}
```

plus an `outputSchema`, and `tools/call` with `{ "id": "1" }` answers
`{ "data": { "book": { "id": "1", "title": "Dune" } } }`.

## The manifest

`operations.documents` is core's `TrustedManifest`, in the three formats `trustedDocuments.manifest`
takes: an object of id to source (GraphQL Code Generator's `persisted-documents.json`, Relay's
persisted queries file), an Apollo persisted query manifest
(`{ format: 'apollo-persisted-query-manifest', version: 1, operations: [{ id, body }] }`), or a
`Map`. It is usually the same object you give `trustedDocuments`, but it does not have to be.
Your client toolchain writes it: core's
[trusted documents guide](https://github.com/softistx/graxia/blob/develop/packages/core/docs/guide/trusted-documents.md)
shows how for each one. A real client manifest holds every operation of the application, so the
first boot lists the ones without a description: narrow it with `include`, or fill `descriptions`.

- One tool per **named** operation. The tool name is the operation name in snake case
  (`BookById` → `book_by_id`, `HTTPStatus` → `http_status`); the title is the operation name.
- **Queries** are tools. **Mutations** are tools only with `mutations: true`.
  **Subscriptions** are skipped: MCP tools answer once.
- `include` picks the operations to offer. An operation it leaves out is not validated and needs no
  description; every document must still parse and name its operations:

```ts
operations: {
	documents: manifest,
	include: ({ name, kind, id }) => kind === 'query' && !name.startsWith('Admin'),
},
```

Everything is checked once, in `createMcp`, against the full schema. It throws one
`GraxiaConfigError` listing **every** problem with its fix, so a manifest is corrected in one pass
(see [troubleshooting](../troubleshooting.md)): an anonymous operation, two operations giving one
tool name, a name starting with `graphql_` or longer than 128 characters, a document that does not
parse or validate, `@defer` or `@stream`, introspection, a missing description, and a
`descriptions` key that names no operation.

## Descriptions

A description is **required**: an agent picks a tool by it. Write it where the operation lives,
with the executable-descriptions syntax graphql 17 parses, or give it by operation name:

```ts
operations: {
	documents: manifest,
	descriptions: { BookById: 'Find a book by its id.' }, // wins over the document's own
},
```

A variable's description becomes the `description` of its property. A variable without one takes
the description of the argument or input field it feeds.

> Your toolchain must keep the descriptions in the manifest. GraphQL Code Generator's client preset
> keeps them when the project's `graphql` is 16.12 or later (flattened to one line); before 16.12
> the sources do not parse with a description, so use `descriptions`. Open
> `persisted-documents.json` to check: the boot error names each operation that lacks one.

## The input schema

JSON Schema 2020-12, `type: "object"`, `additionalProperties: false`, one property per variable.

| GraphQL                        | JSON Schema                                                                      |
| ------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Int`                          | `{ "type": "integer" }`                                                          |
| `Float`                        | `{ "type": "number" }`                                                           |
| `String`, `ID`                 | `{ "type": "string" }`                                                           |
| `Boolean`                      | `{ "type": "boolean" }`                                                          |
| an enum                        | `{ "type": "string", "enum": [...] }`, described values listed in `description`  |
| a list                         | `{ "type": "array", "items": ... }`                                              |
| an input object                | `{ "$ref": "#/$defs/Name" }`, the object under `$defs` (so recursive types work) |
| a `@oneOf` input object        | `oneOf`, one branch per field                                                    |
| a custom scalar                | `{}` with the scalar's description (any JSON value; no `format` is guessed)      |
| nullable (`String`)            | `"type": ["string", "null"]`; for an input object `anyOf` with `null`            |
| non-null without a default     | listed in `required`                                                             |
| a default (`$first: Int = 10`) | `"default": 10`                                                                  |
| a deprecated input field       | `"deprecated": true`                                                             |

### `@constraint`

`@constraint` (from `@graxia/core/agent`) becomes `minLength`, `maxLength`, `minimum`, `maximum`,
`exclusiveMinimum`, `exclusiveMaximum`, `multipleOf`, `pattern`, `format`, and on a list `minItems`
and `maxItems` (the other limits then apply to the items). It is read:

- on **input fields**, inside `$defs`;
- for a **variable**, on the arguments and input fields the variable is used at. A variable used at
  several places gets the tightest bound of each kind; `pattern`, `format` and `multipleOf` are
  kept when the usages agree and left out when they differ.

The schema guides the agent; it is not the check. An argument the schema does not have is refused
(`MCP_UNKNOWN_ARGUMENT`, with the accepted names). The others go to graxia as variables, unchanged,
and graxia's own coercion and your resolvers decide: a wrong argument answers with a GraphQL error
(`Variable "$id" has invalid value: …`, code `BAD_USER_INPUT`) whose fix is
`Correct the arguments: see the tool's input schema.`

## The output schema

```json
{
	"type": "object",
	"properties": {
		"data": {
			"type": ["object", "null"],
			"properties": { "book": { "...": "..." } }
		},
		"errors": {
			"type": "array",
			"items": { "...": "message, path, extensions.code, extensions.fix" }
		}
	}
}
```

`data` follows the selection set, by response key (aliases included): a nullable field also accepts
`null`, lists are arrays, `__typename` is a string, named and inline fragments are merged.
On an interface or a union the fields of every fragment are merged into one object, and a field
selected only for some of the possible types (or under `@skip` / `@include`) is not required:
there is no branch per type. When several selections share one response key
(`... on Book { author { name } } ... on Mag { author { age } }`), a nested key is required only
if every one of them selects it, or one that always applies does. The same key with different
types in two fragments is an `anyOf`.
A custom scalar is `{}`.

The result keeps the shape of the generic tools ([results](./tools.md#results)):
`structuredContent` is `{ data?, errors? }`, `isError` is `true` when there is no `data`.

## Strict trusted documents

With `trustedDocuments` in `strict` mode (the default under `NODE_ENV=production`) the typed tools
are the only tools that run operations: `graphql_query` and `graphql_mutate` are not listed, and a
call answers `PERSISTED_QUERY_ONLY` with a fix naming the typed tools
([tools](./tools.md#trusted-documents)). The typed tools run through `graxia.execute`, in process,
which graxia trusts as it trusts your own server code: the operations are yours, read at boot; the
agent only chooses one and gives its variables. Limits, cost, masking, field rate limits and your
`context` still apply. A strict server without `operations` boots, with `graphql_schema` alone.

## Only the typed tools

```ts
createMcp(graxia, {
	name: 'library',
	operations: { documents: manifest },
	genericTools: false, // no graphql_query, no graphql_mutate
});
```

`graphql_schema` stays, and names the typed tools. `genericTools: false` without `operations`, or
with operations that give no tool, throws: there would be nothing to call. This is the tightest
surface: see [security](./security.md#typed-tools-only).

## Permissions and scopes

- **`can`**: a tool is listed for a caller only when its operation is valid against the schema that
  caller may see. A tool using a field behind a `@needs` they lack is not listed, and calling it
  answers `Tool <name> not found`, exactly like a tool that does not exist.
- **`auth`**: query tools need the read scope (`mcp:read`), mutation tools the write scope
  (`mcp:write`). A read-only token does not see the mutation tools, and calling one is the same 403
  step-up as `graphql_mutate` ([auth](./auth.md#scopes-and-step-up)), unless `can` hides the tool
  from that caller: then it is `Tool <name> not found`.
- Query tools carry `readOnlyHint: true`; mutation tools `readOnlyHint: false, destructiveHint: true`.

## Cost

Parsing, validation and both schemas are computed once, in `createMcp`. Per request only the
filter by the caller's view runs: once for all callers without `can`; with `can`, once per
`tools/list` and `tools/call` request (the view is built, so `can` runs, for those two only:
`initialize`, `ping` and notifications never call it). When `can` throws, nothing typed is listed
and a call answers `The server failed to run the operation. Fix: retry later.`

# @graxia/mcp — Security

Source: packages/mcp/docs/guide/security.md

# Security

## Authentication

Set `auth` and `@graxia/mcp` is an OAuth resource server: bearer tokens, scopes, protected
resource metadata ([the auth guide](./auth.md)). Every request then needs a token your
`verifyToken` accepts, issued for this resource (the audience is checked by default), and
`graphql_mutate` and the typed tools of mutations need the write scope (a 403 naming the tool
called; with `mutations` off they are `Tool … not found`).

Without `auth` nothing authenticates: mount the endpoint behind your own auth (a reverse proxy, a
check in the `Bun.serve` route before `mcp.fetch`) and treat it as you would `/graphql`. Keep
`graphql_mutate` off (`mutations` defaults to `false`) unless the caller is trusted.

```ts
routes: {
	'/mcp': async (request, server) => {
		const principal = await authenticate(request);
		if (!principal) return new Response('Unauthorized', { status: 401 });
		return mcp.fetch(request, { server, principal });
	},
},
```

## `can`

`can(request, serverContext, auth)` (`auth` is the verified token, with `auth` set) returns a function `permission => boolean` (it may be async). The
tools describe and validate against the schema as that caller sees it, so a field behind `@needs`
they lack is "Cannot query field": the agent can neither see it nor ask for it. The `@needs` is
also whatever your own resolvers or plugins enforce at run time: `can` is the view, not the lock.

`can` shapes what the agent sees and may ask for, not the objects a field returns. A union or
interface field the caller sees can still return objects of a type the view hides: the agent cannot
name that type in a fragment, but `__typename` and the interface's fields come back. A resolver of
a union or interface field must itself leave out the objects the caller may not read.

## Typed tools only

`graphql_query` lets an agent write any operation the caller may see. To let it run only
operations you have reviewed, give them as [typed tools](./operations.md) and turn the generic
ones off:

```ts
createMcp(graxia, {
	name: 'library',
	operations: { documents: manifest },
	genericTools: false,
});
```

The agent then chooses a tool and gives its variables; it never sends a document. A typed tool is
listed only when its operation is valid in the caller's view, and a mutation tool needs
`mutations: true` and, with `auth`, the write scope. `operations.documents` is trusted like your
own code: build it from your repository, never from a request.

## Strict trusted documents

`graxia.execute` runs in process and skips the trusted-documents check (it is your own code
calling). `@graxia/mcp` forwards documents written by an agent, so it applies the mode itself:
when `graxia.trustedDocuments.mode` is `strict` (the default under `NODE_ENV=production`),
`graphql_query` and `graphql_mutate` are not listed and a call answers `PERSISTED_QUERY_ONLY`
without running anything. Only the typed tools run, each a document you gave at boot. In `mixed`
mode the generic tools run any document the caller's view allows, as `/graphql` does.

## Origin, Host and DNS rebinding

A browser can be tricked into calling a local MCP server by a hostile page whose domain is
re-pointed at `127.0.0.1` (DNS rebinding): the page then talks to your server as its own origin.
Two checks stop it, both only for a request that carries an `Origin` header:

- the `Origin` must be in `allowedOrigins`, **or**
- it must be the endpoint's own origin **and** the `Host` header must name a hostname of
  `allowedHosts` (default `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `[::1]`). A rebound `evil.example` is its own
  origin, but it is not an allowed host: 403.

A request without `Origin` (a CLI, a server, an IDE) passes: it is not a browser. For a
non-local endpoint set the public hostname, without port:

```ts
createMcp(graxia, { name: 'library', allowedHosts: ['mcp.example.com'] });
```

Behind a proxy that terminates TLS the request reaches Bun as `http://`, so the endpoint's own
origin is `http://…`, not the public one: list the public origin in `allowedOrigins`
(`https://mcp.example.com`) and the hostname in `allowedHosts`. Entries must be exact (a hostname
without port; an origin as `scheme://host[:port]`): `createMcp` throws on one that can never match.

## CORS

A browser client on another origin needs `allowedOrigins: ['https://app.example']`. Its `OPTIONS`
preflight is then answered 204 (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, `-Methods: POST`, `-Headers`
including `content-type`, `authorization`, `mcp-protocol-version` and `mcp-session-id`,
`Vary: Origin`) and every response to it carries `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` and exposes
`WWW-Authenticate`. Preflights never need a token. A preflight from
any other origin is a 403 and gets no CORS header.

## Body size and type

A POST body over the instance's `limits.bodyBytes` (1 MiB by default, read from `graxia.limits`) is
a 413. Only `application/json` is accepted (415 otherwise).

## Failures are reported, not shown

An unexpected failure (a throwing `can`, a failing transport) is sent to `onError` (default
`console.error`) with its cause; the agent only sees a generic message. The default sink skips the
SDK's protocol rejections (messages starting with `Rejected `, a client's own mistake); pass your
own `onError` to see them, or `false` to silence everything.

A document that does not parse is refused by the MCP server itself (`GRAPHQL_PARSE_FAILED`) and never
reaches `graxia.execute`, so a lenient parser set by a plugin cannot run what the visibility checks
have not seen. The checks see the document graphql's own parser reads: a plugin parser
(`setParseFn`) that rewrites a valid document into another one is trusted like any plugin, since it
already decides what runs on `/graphql` too.

CORS preflights echo the headers the browser asks for (`Access-Control-Request-Headers`), so custom
auth headers work from an allowed origin.

## What graxia still enforces

Every operation goes through `graxia.execute`: depth and alias limits, cost, masking of resolver
errors, field rate limits, and your `context`. MCP does not bypass any of them, and it refuses
agent-written documents itself in `strict` trusted-documents mode (above).

# @graxia/mcp — Tools

Source: packages/mcp/docs/guide/tools.md

# Tools

Every tool sees the schema as the caller may see it: with `can`, a field behind `@needs` the caller
lacks does not exist for them (it is neither described nor accepted).

With `operations`, each persisted operation is one more tool, with typed arguments: see
[persisted operations as typed tools](./operations.md). `genericTools: false` removes
`graphql_query` and `graphql_mutate` and keeps `graphql_schema` and the typed tools.

## `graphql_schema`

Input `{ search?: string, types?: string[] }`.

- **No input**: the operations the caller can use (root fields with their arguments and the first
  line of their description, `Query`, and `Mutation` only when `mutations` is on) and the list of
  type names (the `Mutation` root is not offered, nor found by `search`, unless `mutations` is on).
  With `operations` it ends with the typed tools this caller has, and says to prefer them (with
  `genericTools: false`, or in strict trusted-documents mode, that they are the only way to run
  operations).
- **`types`**: the SDL of those types, with descriptions, `@deprecated` and the applied `@needs`,
  `@constraint` and `@errors`, plus the definition of each of those directives used. A name that
  does not exist is listed as unknown, with a fix.
- **`search`**: every word (case-insensitive) must appear in the type's name or description, or in
  a field or enum value name or description. The answer is the SDL of the matching types, at most
  50 (`types` takes at most 50 names too); when more match it says so and tells the agent to narrow the search.

## `graphql_query`

Input `{ query: string, variables?: object, operationName?: string }`. The document is parsed and
validated against the caller's view, then run through `graxia.execute`, so operation limits, cost,
masking and field rate limits apply as they do on HTTP ([trusted documents](#trusted-documents) below).

Introspection (`__schema`, `__type`) is refused: it would show fields `@needs` hides. Use
`graphql_schema`. `__typename` stays allowed. Only the validation rules that decide what the caller
may see run on the view (unknown fields, types and arguments, impossible fragment spreads);
limits, cost and the rest of validation are graxia's, when the operation runs, with graxia's own
codes. A document that does not parse is refused here (the token limit of graxia applies) and never handed to graxia.

### Refusals

| input                                         | `extensions.code`                        | message                                     | fix                                                                                         |
| --------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| a document that does not parse                | `GRAPHQL_PARSE_FAILED`                   | the parser's message                        | correct the syntax                                                                          |
| an unknown or hidden field, type or argument  | `GRAPHQL_VALIDATION_FAILED`              | `Cannot query field "x" on type "Y".`       | call `graphql_schema`, correct the operation                                                |
| `__schema` or `__type`                        | `GRAPHQL_VALIDATION_FAILED`              | graphql's introspection message             | `Use graphql_schema to read the schema.`                                                    |
| a mutation in `graphql_query`                 | `MCP_OPERATION_NOT_ALLOWED`              | `A mutation cannot run in graphql_query.`   | use `graphql_mutate`                                                                        |
| a query in `graphql_mutate`                   | `MCP_OPERATION_NOT_ALLOWED`              | `A query cannot run in graphql_mutate.`     | use `graphql_query`                                                                         |
| a subscription                                | `SUBSCRIPTION_NOT_SUPPORTED`             | `Subscriptions are not available over MCP.` | send a query                                                                                |
| `@defer` or `@stream`                         | `INCREMENTAL_NOT_SUPPORTED`              | `@defer is not available over MCP.`         | remove the directive                                                                        |
| a limit, cost or rate refusal, a bad variable | graxia's own                             | graxia's message                            | graxia's fix                                                                                |
| a plugin answered with its own response       | the plugin's, when its body has `errors` | the plugin's                                | the plugin's                                                                                |
| a plugin response with no `errors`, shutdown  | `MCP_EXECUTION_REFUSED`                  | the `graxia.execute` message                | `Retry later; if it persists, the server is shutting down or a plugin refused the request.` |

The typed tools add `MCP_UNKNOWN_ARGUMENT` ([troubleshooting](../troubleshooting.md)), and `auth` adds
`MCP_UNAUTHORIZED`, `MCP_INSUFFICIENT_SCOPE` and `MCP_TOKEN_IN_URL`
([troubleshooting auth](../troubleshooting-auth.md)). `McpErrorCode` (an exported type) is the union
of the codes `@graxia/mcp` emits.

`operationName` picks the operation: only the selected one is checked against the tool's kind, so a
document holding a query and a mutation runs its query in `graphql_query`.

## `graphql_mutate`

Listed only with `mutations: true`; same input. A query is refused with a fix pointing to
`graphql_query`. With `mutations` off the tool does not exist: calling it is a JSON-RPC error
(`Tool graphql_mutate not found`). With `auth`, it is listed only for a token with the write scope
(`mcp:write` by default), and a read-only token calling it gets a 403 step-up
([auth](./auth.md#scopes-and-step-up)).

## Results

```json
{ "data": { "books": [{ "title": "Dune" }] } }
```

- `structuredContent` is the GraphQL result (`{ data?, errors? }`); `content[0].text` is the same JSON.
- `isError` is `true` when there is no `data` (the operation did not run, or failed before any
  field). A result with `data` and field `errors` is not an error call: the agent reads `errors`.
- Every error has `extensions.code` and `extensions.fix`. A masked failure keeps graxia's
  `INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR` code and its fix ("Retry later; quote the correlationId…"); the message
  and cause never leak.

## Trusted documents

With `trustedDocuments` in `strict` mode (the default in production) graxia runs no document a
client writes, and neither does the MCP server: `graphql_query` and `graphql_mutate` are **not
listed**, and a call answers `Only persisted documents are allowed.` with the code
`PERSISTED_QUERY_ONLY` and a fix naming the typed tools the caller has. `graphql_schema` stays.
The [typed tools](./operations.md) of `operations` run: they are the documents you persisted.
Without `operations` a strict server boots with `graphql_schema` alone, so nothing can be run:
`createMcp` reports it once through `onError` ("graxia runs trusted documents in strict mode and
`operations` gives no tool"). Pass `operations`. In `mixed` mode the generic tools are unchanged.

## Cost of `can`

The caller view is built lazily, by the tool that needs it: `initialize`, `ping`, notifications
and `tools/list` never build it. Without `can` it is computed once, on the first tool call. With
`can`, it is computed on every tool call (the schema is printed and rebuilt for that caller's
permissions). It is cheap for a small schema; for a large one, keep `can` fast and expect a few
milliseconds per request. With `operations` the view decides which typed tools exist, so
`tools/list` and every `tools/call` build it (still once for all callers without `can`);
`initialize`, `ping` and notifications still do not.

# @graxia/mcp — Troubleshooting auth

Source: packages/mcp/docs/troubleshooting-auth.md

# Troubleshooting auth

The answers of `auth` ([the auth guide](./guide/auth.md)) and its boot errors, each headed by the
message or code you see. Everything else is in [troubleshooting](./troubleshooting.md).

## 401 `Unauthorized: no bearer token.` (`MCP_UNAUTHORIZED`)

Header: `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="…", scope="mcp:read"`.

`auth` is set and the request has no `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. A client with OAuth support
follows `resource_metadata` to the authorization server; otherwise send the token yourself. Another
scheme is not read: `Authorization: DPoP …` gets this answer too (DPoP is not supported).

## 401 `Unauthorized: the access token is invalid.` (`MCP_UNAUTHORIZED`)

Header: `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token", …`, as for the next five entries.

`verifyToken` resolved `undefined`: it does not know the token (a bad signature, another issuer,
revoked). Get a new token from the authorization server.

## 401 `Unauthorized: the access token has expired.`

The `expiresAt` your verifier returned is in the past. Refresh the token.

## 401 `Unauthorized: the access token was issued for another resource.`

The `audience` your verifier returned does not contain `auth.resource` (a fragment and one trailing
slash are ignored). The client must ask for a token for the same URL as `auth.resource` (the
`resource` parameter, RFC 8707). Check the `aud` claim of the token first.

## 401 `Unauthorized: the access token carries no audience.`

`verifyToken` returned no `audience`, and the audience is checked by default. Return the token's
`aud`, or, when your verifier already refuses tokens issued for another resource, opt out with
`audience: 'verifier'` ([the auth guide](./guide/auth.md#audience)).

## 401 `Unauthorized: the verifier returned an unusable expiry (expiresAt is in seconds).`

`onError` got `createMcp: verifyToken returned expiresAt …, and expiresAt is in seconds since the
epoch`. `expiresAt` is not a finite number or is above 1e11, which is a date in milliseconds.
Return the `exp` claim as is, or `Math.floor(date.getTime() / 1000)`; leave it out when the token
has no expiry.

## 401 `Unauthorized: the verifier returned no scopes.`

`onError` got `createMcp: verifyToken must return scopes`. The info has no `scopes` array: return
`{ scopes: [...] }`, an empty list for a token with none.

## 503 `The access token could not be verified: the token verifier failed.`

With `Retry-After: 5`. `verifyToken` threw (an introspection endpoint or a key store is down); the
error went to `onError`. A throw is an outage, never a 401: resolve `undefined` for a bad token.

**Every expired token answers 503: your verifier throws on a bad token.** A JWT library that
rejects an expired, badly signed or wrong-audience token by throwing (jose's `jwtVerify`) turns
each of them into a 503 the client retries instead of refreshing its token. Catch the library's
invalid-token errors in `verifyToken` and resolve `undefined`; rethrow the rest (a JWKS fetch, an
introspection call), as in [the auth guide](./guide/auth.md#verifytoken).

## A 401 or 503 whose body is not JSON-RPC

`verifyToken` resolved a `Response` (a verifier that builds its own refusals): it is sent as is.
Read that library's documentation for its meaning.

## `Forbidden: the token lacks mcp:read.` (`MCP_INSUFFICIENT_SCOPE`)

A 403 with `error="insufficient_scope", scope="mcp:read"`. Ask the authorization server for
`mcp:read` (or your `scopes.read`).

## `Forbidden: graphql_mutate needs the scope mcp:write.` (`MCP_INSUFFICIENT_SCOPE`)

A 403 with `error="insufficient_scope", scope="mcp:read mcp:write"`. The message names the tool
called, so a typed tool answers `Forbidden: rename_book needs the scope mcp:write.`. A read-only token called a tool that writes from a stale
tool list. Re-authorize with both scopes (the challenge's `scope`); these tools are not listed for
a token without `mcp:write`. With `mutations` off there is no 403: the call gets
`Tool graphql_mutate not found`. A mutation tool `can` hides from the caller gets no 403 either,
and in strict trusted-documents mode `graphql_mutate` answers `PERSISTED_QUERY_ONLY`, not the 403.

## `createMcp: auth.resource must be an absolute URL (got "…").`

Thrown by `createMcp` at startup. Pass the public URL of the MCP endpoint, scheme included:
`resource: 'https://api.example.com/mcp'`.

## `createMcp: auth.resource must have no query and no fragment (got "…").`

Thrown at startup. A resource identifier is the endpoint's URL alone (RFC 8707): remove the `?…`
and the `#…`.

## `createMcp: auth.authorizationServers is empty.`

Thrown at startup. List the issuer URL of the authorization server that issues the tokens:
`authorizationServers: ['https://auth.example.com']`.

## `createMcp: auth.authorizationServers must hold absolute URLs (got "…").`

Thrown at startup. Every entry is an issuer URL with its scheme (`https://auth.example.com`, not
`auth.example.com`).

## 400 `The access token is in the query string.` (`MCP_TOKEN_IN_URL`)

`?access_token=…` is refused (OAuth 2.1). Send `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.

# @graxia/mcp — Troubleshooting

Source: packages/mcp/docs/troubleshooting.md

# Troubleshooting

Each entry is headed by the message or code you see. The 401, 403 and 503 answers of `auth` and its
boot errors are in [troubleshooting auth](./troubleshooting-auth.md).

## 403 `Origin https://… is not allowed.`

A browser client sent an `Origin` that is not in `allowedOrigins` and is not the endpoint's own.

```ts
createMcp(graxia, { name: 'library', allowedOrigins: ['https://app.example'] });
```

A CLI or server client sends no `Origin` and is not affected.

## 403 `Host … is not allowed.`

The request is same-origin but its `Host` header names a hostname outside `allowedHosts` (default
`localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `[::1]`): the DNS-rebinding guard. Set the endpoint's public hostname,
without port. Behind a proxy, list the hostname the browser uses.

```ts
createMcp(graxia, { name: 'library', allowedHosts: ['mcp.example.com'] });
```

## 405 `GET is not supported: this endpoint is stateless.`

Also `DELETE is not supported: this endpoint is stateless.` (and any other method but `POST`). The
endpoint has no server-to-client stream and no sessions. Clients send `POST`; a client that probes
with `GET` or `DELETE` and goes on after the 405 is working as intended.

## 413 `The request body is larger than … bytes.`

The body is over `limits.bodyBytes` of the graxia instance, which the MCP endpoint reads from
`graxia.limits`. Send a smaller request or raise it on `createGraxia`; both endpoints follow.

## 415 `The request body must be application/json.`

Send `Content-Type: application/json`.

## 500 `The MCP server failed to handle the request.`

The transport failed (a broken body stream, a bug). The cause is not sent; it went to `onError`
(default `console.error`). Pass your own to log it:

```ts
createMcp(graxia, { name: 'library', onError: (error) => logger.error(error) });
```

## `createMcp: no serverContext for this request; the MCP handler ran outside fetch.`

The handler was called without going through `mcp.fetch`. Always mount `mcp.fetch`.

## `Cannot query field "x" on type "Y"` for a field that exists

Reported with `extensions.code` `GRAPHQL_VALIDATION_FAILED`.

The field is behind `@needs` and `can` says the caller lacks the permission, or `can` is not what
you meant: the view is built from `can`'s answer. Check it with `graphql_schema` as that caller.

## `graphql_mutate` is missing from the list with `mutations: true`

With `auth`, it is listed only for a token with the write scope (`mcp:write` by default). When
graxia runs trusted documents in `strict` mode it is never listed, like `graphql_query`.

## `GraphQL introspection has been disabled…` / `Use graphql_schema to read the schema.`

`__schema` and `__type` are refused over MCP: they would show fields `@needs` hides. Call
`graphql_schema` (no input, `types` or `search`). `__typename` is allowed.

## `No type matches "x".` (or `Empty search.`)

`graphql_schema` with `search` found no type or field of that name in the caller's view (a hidden
type is not found either); `Empty search.` means `search` was blank. Call `graphql_schema` with
no input for the type names, then search a word of one of them.

## `# Unknown type X. Fix: call graphql_schema with no input to list the type names you can use.`

`graphql_schema` was asked for a type the caller cannot see or that does not exist. The `Mutation`
root is also unknown unless `mutations: true`. Call it with no input for the list.

## `A mutation cannot run in graphql_query.`

Use `graphql_mutate` (listed only with `mutations: true`). The reverse, `A query cannot run in
graphql_mutate.`, means use `graphql_query`. Code `MCP_OPERATION_NOT_ALLOWED`. In a document with
several operations, `operationName` picks the one checked.

## `Subscriptions are not available over MCP.`

Code `SUBSCRIPTION_NOT_SUPPORTED`. Send a query, or poll the same query again.

## `@defer is not available over MCP.` (or `@stream`)

Code `INCREMENTAL_NOT_SUPPORTED`. Remove the directive: the tool returns one complete JSON result.

## A parse failure (`Syntax Error: …`, `Document contains more than N tokens.`)

Code `GRAPHQL_PARSE_FAILED`, raised by the MCP server before `graxia.execute`: correct the syntax at the position the error gives, or
raise `limits.tokens` on `createGraxia` for a very large document.

## `Tool graphql_mutate not found`

It is listed only with `mutations: true` (and, with `auth`, for a token with the write scope).
`Tool graphql_query not found`: `genericTools` is `false`; call a typed tool.

## `Tool book_by_id not found` for an operation of the manifest

The tool is not offered to this caller: its operation uses a field `can` hides from them, it is a
mutation without `mutations: true`, `include` left it out, or it is a subscription. The answer is
the same as for a tool that does not exist. Call `graphql_schema` for the typed tools you have.

## `createMcp: operations has 1 problem:` (or `N problems:`)

One error lists every problem of `operations`, one per line, each ending with its fix:

- `document "a1" holds an anonymous operation: a tool needs a name.` Name it and regenerate.
- `BookById (document "a1") has no description: …` Write `"""…"""` above the operation, or set
  `operations.descriptions.BookById`. A toolchain that drops descriptions needs the option.
- `operations.descriptions.bookById matches no operation of operations.documents (there is
  BookById: names are case-sensitive).` Rename or remove the key.
- `BookById (document "a1") and Book_by_id (document "a2") both give the tool name book_by_id.`
  Rename one, or leave one out with `include`.
- `GraphqlQuery (document "a1") gives the tool name graphql_query, and graphql_* names are the
  generic tools'.` Rename the operation, or leave it out.
- `… gives a tool name of 140 characters, and MCP allows 128.` Rename the operation.
- `document "a1" does not parse: Syntax Error: …` Regenerate the manifest.
- `BookById (document "a1") is not valid against the schema: Cannot query field …` The manifest is
  older than the schema (or belongs to another server): regenerate it.
- `Types (document "a1") selects __schema or __type: introspection is not offered over MCP, …`
  Leave the operation out with `include`: an agent reads the schema with `graphql_schema`.
- `BookById (document "a1") uses @defer, which is not available over MCP: …` (or `@stream`).
- `document "a1" is not a GraphQL source string.` Map every id to the text of its document.
- `operations.documents is not a manifest.` Pass a `Map`, an object of id to source, or an Apollo
  persisted query manifest.
- `genericTools is false and operations gives no tool: …` Without the generic tools an agent needs
  at least one typed tool: check `documents` and `include` (mutations need `mutations: true`).

An operation `include` leaves out, a subscription, and a mutation without `mutations: true` is not
validated and needs no description; every document must still parse and name its operations.

## `createMcp: graxia runs trusted documents in strict mode and `operations` gives no tool: …`

Reported once through `onError` at boot (not thrown: the same code boots in development). graxia's
`trustedDocuments` is `strict` (the default under `NODE_ENV=production`), so `graphql_query` and
`graphql_mutate` are not listed, and with no `operations` there is no typed tool: agents read the
schema and run nothing. Fix: pass the persisted documents.

```ts
createMcp(graxia, { name: 'library', operations: { documents: manifest } });
```

## `createMcp: allowedHosts entry "…" can never match` / `allowedOrigins entry "…" can never match`

Thrown at startup. `allowedHosts` takes hostnames only (`mcp.example.com`, `[::1]`), without
scheme, port or path; `allowedOrigins` takes exactly `scheme://host[:port]`, with no path and no
trailing slash. The message gives the corrected value.

```ts
createMcp(graxia, {
	name: 'library',
	allowedHosts: ['mcp.example.com'], // not 'mcp.example.com:3000'
	allowedOrigins: ['https://app.example'], // not 'https://app.example/'
});
```

## `createMcp: genericTools is false and there is no operations: …`

Pass `operations: { documents: manifest }`, or remove `genericTools: false`.

## `book_by_id does not take the argument extra.` (`MCP_UNKNOWN_ARGUMENT`)

A typed tool was called with an argument that is not a variable of its operation. The fix names
the arguments it accepts; they are the `properties` of its `inputSchema` in `tools/list`.

## A typed tool answers `Variable "$id" …` (`BAD_USER_INPUT`)

An argument is missing or has the wrong type: graxia checks the arguments as the operation's
variables. The fix is `Correct the arguments: see the tool's input schema.`

## `Forbidden: rename_book needs the scope mcp:write.` (`MCP_INSUFFICIENT_SCOPE`)

A 403 `insufficient_scope`: a mutation typed tool was called with a read-only token, the same
step-up as `graphql_mutate` ([auth troubleshooting](./troubleshooting-auth.md)).

## `Only persisted documents are allowed.` (`PERSISTED_QUERY_ONLY`) from `graphql_query`

graxia's `trustedDocuments` is `strict` (the default under `NODE_ENV=production`), so the server
runs no document an agent writes: `graphql_query` and `graphql_mutate` are not listed and a call
answers this refusal, whose fix names the typed tools the caller has. Give the agent
[typed tools](./guide/operations.md) (`operations`); without them only `graphql_schema` is there.

## `graxia.execute: the request ended with an HTTP … response instead of a result; see error.response.`

Code `MCP_EXECUTION_REFUSED`, with the fix `Retry later; if it persists, the server is shutting
down or a plugin refused the request.` A plugin answered with its own response whose body has no
`errors`, or the server is shutting down. A plugin response with `errors` reaches the agent as
they are (its code and fix, e.g. `UNAUTHENTICATED`), so shape your plugin's refusal as
`{ errors: [{ message, extensions: { code, fix } }] }`.

## `The server failed to run the operation. Fix: retry later.`

An unexpected failure inside the tool (a throwing `can`, a bug); its cause is not sent. It went to
`onError` and, for the operation itself, to graxia's `onUnexpected`. When `can` throws,
`tools/list` also answers without the typed tools, and a call to one gets this answer: the cause
is in `onError`.

# @graxia/redis — @graxia/redis

Source: packages/redis/README.md

# @graxia/redis

Redis PubSub, cache and field rate limit for graxia, on [`@softistx/redis`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@softistx/redis)
(one shared client per URI, one reconnecting subscriber connection, server-timed rate limits) over Bun's built-in
Redis client. No ioredis or node-redis.

## Install

```sh
bun add @graxia/redis @graxia/core @softistx/redis zod
```

## Requirements

- [Bun](https://bun.sh) 1.4.4 or later (the `engines` field), and a Redis server.
- `@graxia/core` and `@softistx/redis` (`^0.24.0`) as peer dependencies. `@softistx/redis` requires `zod` as a peer (its type declarations import it): install both, `bun add @softistx/redis zod`.
- With `url`, the client is shared per URI with every other `connectRedis` of your process, which must use the same options for
  that URI; if another module connects it with options, pass its client as `{ client }`.
- `typescript` is an optional peer, for types. Use `"moduleResolution": "bundler"` in your
  `tsconfig.json`; `nodenext` is not supported.

## Migrating from 0.1

0.2 has four breaks, detailed in the [guide](./docs/guide/redis.md#migrating-from-01):

1. Topics follow core's Yoga-shaped PubSub: `subscribe('post:42', { signal })` becomes `subscribe('post', '42')`.
2. `@softistx/redis` (and its peer `zod`) must be installed.
3. A cache `prefix` is used with exactly one trailing `:`; one without it writes new keys.
4. With `url`, adapters of one URI share one client, so the same URI needs the same options everywhere.

Exports: `redisPubSub`, `redisCache`, `redisFieldLimit` and the types `RedisConnection`, `RedisPubSub`, `RedisPubSubOptions`,
`RedisCacheOptions`, `RedisFieldLimit`, `RedisFieldLimitOptions`.

## PubSub: swap memory for Redis

`redisPubSub` implements the same `PubSub` contract as `createPubSub` (Yoga's shape: `subscribe('post', id)`, `publish('post', id, payload)`), so resolvers
and `pipe` / `filter` / `map` do not change. A topic with an id is the Redis channel `<prefix>topic:id`. Subscribers in other processes receive what you publish.

```ts
import { filter, pipe } from '@graxia/core';
import { redisPubSub } from '@graxia/redis';

type Topics = {
	post: [id: string, payload: { id: string; published: boolean }];
};
const pubsub = redisPubSub<Topics>({ url: process.env.REDIS_URL });

// the Subscription resolver: the engine returns the iterator when the client leaves
const resolvers = {
	Subscription: {
		postPublished: {
			subscribe: () =>
				pipe(
					pubsub.subscribe('post', '42'),
					filter((post) => post.published),
				),
			resolve: (post: { id: string }) => post,
		},
	},
};

await pubsub.publish('post', '42', { id: '42', published: true });
await pubsub.dispose(); // on shutdown
```

Options (all optional):

| Option                      | Default                                    | Meaning                                                                             |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `url`                       | `REDIS_URL`, then `redis://localhost:6379` | Connection; the client is shared per URI (`connectRedis`) and let go on `dispose()` |
| `client`                    |                                            | A `RedisClient` you own instead of `url`; never closed by us                        |
| `prefix`                    | `graxia:`                                  | Prepended to every channel                                                          |
| `bufferSize`                | 1000                                       | Events buffered per subscriber; past it the oldest is dropped                       |
| `onOverflow`                |                                            | Called once per dropped event with `{ topic, dropped }`                             |
| `serialize` / `deserialize` | `JSON.stringify` / `JSON.parse`            | Payload codec                                                                       |
| `onError`                   |                                            | Connection, subscription and payload errors                                         |

## Cache

Options: `url` (`REDIS_URL`, then `redis://localhost:6379`, through `connectRedis`), `client` (as above) and `prefix`
(default `graxia:cache:`, used with exactly one trailing `:`). Keys are `graxia:cache:<key>` by default; `app` and `app:` both give `app:<key>`.

`redisCache` implements core's `KeyValueCache<string>`; `createMemoryCache` is its in-process twin. It is also the store of core's automatic persisted
queries: `trustedDocuments: { store: redisCache({ url }) }` shares registrations across processes (`url` is optional: `REDIS_URL`, then `redis://localhost:6379`, shared per URI).

```ts
import { redisCache } from '@graxia/redis';

const cache = redisCache({
	url: process.env.REDIS_URL,
	prefix: 'graxia:cache:',
});
await cache.set('greeting', 'hello', { ttlMs: 60_000 }); // SET ... PX 60000
await cache.get('greeting'); // 'hello'
await cache.delete('greeting'); // true when a key was removed
await cache.dispose?.(); // lets go of a shared client it opened; a `client` you passed stays open
```

## Field rate limit

`redisFieldLimit` is a `FieldLimit` for core's `fieldRateLimit` that every process shares: a GCRA bucket on
`@softistx/redis`'s `consumeRateLimit`, timed by the Redis server (no common clock needed).

```ts
import { fieldRateLimit } from '@graxia/core';
import { redisFieldLimit } from '@graxia/redis';

fieldRateLimit({
	fields: {
		search: redisFieldLimit({
			url: process.env.REDIS_URL,
			limit: 30,
			windowMs: 60_000,
		}),
	},
});
```

Options: `limit`, `windowMs` (integers of 1 or more), `burst` (default `limit`), `prefix` (default `graxia:limit:`; keys are `graxia:limit:<key>` by default, and `app` and `app:` both give `app:<key>`), `timeoutMs`
(default 1000), `onError`, `url` / `client`. A cost over the burst is refused at once with a `retryAfter` of one window; a cost of 0
spends nothing. A Redis error goes to `onError` and the call is let through (fail open). Unlike `memoryFieldLimit`'s fixed
window, the bucket refills continuously; the guide compares them.

## Delivery guarantees

Redis PubSub is at most once, and graxia adds nothing on top:

- One dedicated subscriber connection (`@softistx/redis`'s `createRawSubscriber`), opened on the first `subscribe()`, carries one
  `SUBSCRIBE` per topic, shared by every local subscriber and dropped with the last.
- `publish()` never rejects: a failing command or `serialize` goes to `onError` and `publish` resolves, so an un-awaited call is safe. A topic without payload (`[]`) publishes and delivers `null`.
- Events published while a connection is down are lost. Iterators stay open across a reconnect
  and receive later events; a connection Bun gives up on is reopened with a backoff (250 ms doubling to 10 s).
- `publish()` and `ready()` wait for this instance's own pending SUBSCRIBEs, so they can wait while
  the subscriber connection is down; `ready()` never rejects, and `dispose()` waits at most one
  second for them.
- Events published by another process just after `subscribe()` returns may arrive before the
  server registered the subscription. `await pubsub.ready()` waits for the `SUBSCRIBE`s issued so
  far. `publish` on the same instance waits for its own pending subscriptions, so a local
  subscribe-then-publish is delivered.
- A payload that fails to deserialize is skipped and reported to `onError`, never thrown into an
  iterator. Errors of the connection also go to `onError`.

## Documentation

See [`docs/`](./docs): the [guide](./docs/guide/redis.md), [troubleshooting](./docs/troubleshooting.md)
and the [roadmap](./docs/roadmap.md).

# @graxia/redis — Redis PubSub, cache and field rate limit

Source: packages/redis/docs/guide/redis.md

# Redis PubSub, cache and field rate limit

## Connections

Both adapters take `{ url }` or `{ client }`, never both (see [troubleshooting](../troubleshooting.md)).

- `url` (default: `REDIS_URL`, then `redis://localhost:6379`): the adapter calls `@softistx/redis`'s `connectRedis`
  on first use, so every adapter (and every other module of your process) on the same URI shares **one**
  `RedisClient`; `dispose()` lets go of the shared client (it closes with its last holder), and any later use of the adapter
  rejects with `used after dispose()`. A connect that fails is
  retried by the next call.
- `client`: your `RedisClient`. The adapter uses it to publish (or for cache commands) and never
  closes it. `redisPubSub` also opens one extra connection for subscriptions (`createRawSubscriber` duplicates
  the client), because a subscribed connection cannot run other commands; that one it closes.

`@softistx/redis` is a peer dependency (range `^0.24.0`), and it needs `zod` (its type declarations import it): `bun add @softistx/redis zod`.

## PubSub

```ts
import { createGraxia, createSchema } from '@graxia/core';
import { redisPubSub } from '@graxia/redis';

const pubsub = redisPubSub<{ tick: [payload: number] }>({
	url: process.env.REDIS_URL,
	onError: (error) => console.error('redis', error),
});

const schema = createSchema<{ signal: AbortSignal }>()({
	typeDefs: 'type Query { ok: Boolean } type Subscription { tick: Int! }',
	resolvers: {
		Query: { ok: () => true },
		Subscription: {
			tick: {
				subscribe: () => pubsub.subscribe('tick'),
				resolve: (n: number) => n,
			},
		},
	},
});
const graxia = createGraxia({ schema });
```

The pub/sub `prefix` is used as given (default `graxia:`): pass `'app:'`, not `'app'`, which would name the channel `apptick`.

Any process using the same Redis and `prefix` can call `pubsub.publish('tick', 1)`; every
subscription on every instance receives it.

### Subscribing is shared

The first local subscriber of a topic sends `SUBSCRIBE <prefix><topic>`; further local subscribers
reuse it; the last one leaving (an abort, `return()`, a `break`) sends `UNSUBSCRIBE`. Topics that are
template literals work, since they are concrete strings at runtime.

### When is a subscription live?

`subscribe()` returns at once, before Redis acknowledges. Two consequences:

- On the same instance, `publish` waits for pending `SUBSCRIBE`s, so subscribe-then-publish is
  delivered, as with the memory PubSub.
- An event another process publishes in that window can be missed. `await pubsub.ready()` resolves
  once the commands issued so far are done; call it before signalling that events may flow, or in
  tests.

### Reconnect

Bun reconnects a lost connection on its own (`autoReconnect`, up to `maxRetries`, default 20) but
does not restore its subscriptions. The raw subscriber subscribes again to every active topic on each
`onconnect`, so open iterators keep receiving, once per message. Events published while disconnected are
lost: Redis PubSub is at most once. When Bun gives up (`maxRetries` reached), or Redis was down at the first
`subscribe()`, the subscriber opens a new connection itself after a backoff (250 ms doubling to 10 s) and
subscribes again; the error goes to `onError`. Subscriptions need no restart.

### Waiting while disconnected

`publish()` and `ready()` wait for this instance's own pending SUBSCRIBE/UNSUBSCRIBE commands, so they can
wait while the subscriber connection is down. `ready()` never rejects (failures go to `onError`).
`dispose()` waits at most one second for those commands, so shutdown never hangs.

### Errors

`onError` receives connection errors, failed `SUBSCRIBE` commands and payloads whose `deserialize`
threw (the message is skipped). Nothing is thrown into an iterator. `publish` never rejects: when
Redis rejects the command or `serialize` throws, the error goes to `onError` and `publish` resolves,
so an un-awaited `publish(...)`, as in Yoga, is safe.

### Shutdown

`await pubsub.dispose()` ends every iterator, closes the subscriber connection (and lets go of the shared client
when it opened it; it closes with its last holder) and turns later `publish()` into a no-op and `subscribe()` into a finished iterator.

### Channels and ids

Typed topics are Yoga's: `[payload]` or `[id, payload]`. A topic with an id is the Redis channel
`<prefix>topic:id` (`publish('post', '42', p)` goes to `graxia:post:42`), with one `SUBSCRIBE` per
channel. Coming from 0.1, see [Migrating from 0.1](#migrating-from-01).

## Cache

`redisCache` is a `@softistx/redis` raw cache: it stores strings under `graxia:cache:<key>` by default. A prefix is used with exactly one trailing `:`
(`graxia:cache:<key>` by default; `app` and `app:` both give `app:<key>`) and needs at least one character before it. A `ttlMs` becomes `PX`;
a `set` without one clears a previous expiry. `delete` resolves true when a key was removed.

## Field rate limit

`redisFieldLimit({ limit, windowMs, burst?, prefix?, url? | client? })` is a core `FieldLimit` for `fieldRateLimit`,
on `consumeRateLimit` (GCRA, timed by the Redis server). All processes on one Redis share the counters. A field with
cost `n` spends `n` units at once; a cost over `burst` is refused immediately with `retryAfter` of one window. Keys are
`graxia:limit:<key>` by default; `app` and `app:` both give `app:<key>`. `await limit.dispose()` lets go of the shared client it opened (it closes with its last holder); the
limit then rejects with `used after dispose()`.

Options: `limit`, `windowMs`, `burst` (default `limit`), `prefix` (default `graxia:limit:`, never empty), `timeoutMs` (default 1000,
how long one check waits for Redis, connecting included), `onError`, `url` / `client`. `limit`, `windowMs`, `burst` and `timeoutMs` are
integers of 1 or more; `burst × windowMs` must be at most 9 007 199 254 740 and an empty bucket must refill in under ten
years (`burst × windowMs ÷ limit`), else a `GraxiaConfigError`.

**Redis outage: fail open.** A Redis error (down, timeout) goes to `onError` (nothing is logged without it) and the call is
let through, so a limit never takes the API down with Redis. Misuse (`used after dispose()`, a URI connected with other
options) is not an outage and still rejects.

### `redisFieldLimit` and `memoryFieldLimit`

|                             | `memoryFieldLimit`                     | `redisFieldLimit`                                                                              |
| --------------------------- | -------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Shared by processes         | no, one process                        | yes, one Redis                                                                                 |
| Algorithm                   | fixed window                           | GCRA bucket, timed by the Redis server                                                         |
| Refill                      | the whole window at once, when it ends | one unit per `windowMs / limit`, continuously                                                  |
| Burst                       | `limit` per window                     | `burst` (default `limit`) at once; with the default, up to about 2 × `limit` within one window |
| `retryAfter`                | time until the window resets           | time until this call would be allowed                                                          |
| Cost 0                      | spends nothing, allowed                | spends nothing, allowed (no Redis call)                                                        |
| Cost over the limit / burst | refused (`retryAfter` of one window)   | refused (`retryAfter` of one window)                                                           |
| Backend outage              | n/a                                    | fail open, reported to `onError`                                                               |

## Migrating from 0.1

0.2 has four breaks:

1. **Topics.** `subscribe('post:42', { signal })` becomes `subscribe('post', '42')` (no signal: the engine returns the
   iterator when the operation stops), and the topic type ``{ [k: `post:${string}`]: Post }`` becomes
   `{ post: [id: string, payload: Post] }`; this follows core's Yoga-shaped PubSub. Channel names on Redis are unchanged,
   so old and new processes still talk during a rolling deploy.
2. **Peer.** Install `@softistx/redis` (range `^0.24.0`) and `zod`, which its type declarations import: `bun add @softistx/redis zod`.
3. **Cache prefix.** A prefix is used with exactly one trailing `:`. A prefix that does not end in `:` writes new keys
   (`app:<key>` instead of `app<key>`); entries written by 0.1 are no longer read and expire or can be deleted. A prefix
   that already ends in `:` (the default `graxia:cache:`) keeps its keys. A prefix with no character before its `:`
   (`''` or `':'`) throws a `GraxiaConfigError`.
4. **Shared client.** With `url`, every adapter of one URI shares one client, and `connectRedis` options apply
   process-wide: the same URI must be connected with the same options everywhere (see
   [troubleshooting](../troubleshooting.md)).

`redisPubSub`, `redisCache`, their other options, return types and wire formats are the same.

## Testing against Redis

The package's own Redis specs run when `REDIS_URL` is set and are skipped otherwise:

```sh
docker run -d --rm --name redis-test -p 6379:6379 redis:8-alpine
REDIS_URL=redis://localhost:6379 bun test
docker stop redis-test
```

For application code, use `createPubSub` and `createMemoryCache` in unit tests and Redis in
integration tests; the contracts are the same.

# @graxia/redis — Troubleshooting

Source: packages/redis/docs/troubleshooting.md

# Troubleshooting

The errors a consumer can hit, headed by the message as it appears.

## @graxia/redis: pass either "url" or "client", not both

`redisPubSub`, `redisCache` or `redisFieldLimit` received both `url` and `client` (a `GraxiaConfigError`). Pass a `url` and
the adapter owns its connection, or pass your `client` and you own it.

```ts
redisPubSub({ url: process.env.REDIS_URL }); // or
redisPubSub({ client: myRedisClient });
```

## Connection closed (`ERR_REDIS_CONNECTION_CLOSED`)

Redis is unreachable (wrong `url`, server down, connection refused). Bun's `RedisError` (code
`ERR_REDIS_CONNECTION_CLOSED`) says `Connection has failed`, `Connection closed`, or
`Max reconnection attempts reached` once it has retried `maxRetries` times
(default 20). `publish()` and the cache methods reject with it; for `redisPubSub` the same error also
reaches `onError`, since the subscriber connection fails too. Check the `url` (or `REDIS_URL`) and that
the server listens there.

## Subscriptions stop after a Redis outage

Bun reconnects on its own and `redisPubSub` subscribes again; after `maxRetries` (default 20)
Bun gives up and reports through `onclose`; the error reaches your `onError`, and the subscriber
opens a new connection itself after a backoff (250 ms doubling to 10 s) and subscribes again.
Events published while disconnected are lost. Expect a few `onError` calls during a long outage.

## A subscriber misses the first event

Another process published in the short window before Redis registered `SUBSCRIBE`. Await
`pubsub.ready()` before telling publishers to start; on the same instance `publish` already waits.

## @graxia/redis: <uri> is already connected by another module with other options; pass that client as { client }

A `GraxiaConfigError` (its `cause` is `@softistx/redis`'s `RedisError` with code `URI_CONFLICT`: `connectRedis: this URI is already connected with other
options`). `@softistx/redis` shares one client per URI, so `url` adapters (and any other `connectRedis` of your process)
must use the same URI with the same options. `@graxia/redis` passes none: if another module connects the URI with
options (`maxRetries`, `tls`), open the client there and pass it as `client`. The error depends on the order of the
calls: whoever connects second is refused, and that can be your application's own call rather than the adapter's. The
URI's credentials are never in the message.

```ts
import { connectRedis } from '@softistx/redis';

const redis = await connectRedis(url, { maxRetries: 3 });
redisPubSub({ client: redis.client });
```

## @graxia/redis: used after dispose()

An adapter that opened its client from a `url` was used after `dispose()` (a `GraxiaConfigError`). It does not
reconnect on its own: create a new adapter.

```ts
const pubsub = redisPubSub({ url: process.env.REDIS_URL });
await pubsub.dispose();
const next = redisPubSub({ url: process.env.REDIS_URL }); // a new adapter, a new hold on the shared client
```

## @graxia/redis: redisCache prefix must hold at least one character before its ":"

`redisCache({ prefix: '' })` or `prefix: ':'` (a `GraxiaConfigError`): the prefix names the cache, and `@softistx/redis`
builds keys as `<name>:<key>`. Give it a name, `app` or `app:`, or leave it out for `graxia:cache:`.

## @graxia/redis: redisFieldLimit prefix must hold at least one character before its ":"

`redisFieldLimit({ prefix: '' })` or `prefix: ':'` (a `GraxiaConfigError`): every key would start with a bare `:`, and
limits of unrelated features could collide. Give it a name, `app` or `app:`, or leave it out for `graxia:limit:`.

## redisFieldLimit: limit must be an integer of 1 or more

Also `windowMs` and `burst` (a `GraxiaConfigError`, thrown when the limit is created). They are whole numbers of 1 or
more: `limit` units per `windowMs` milliseconds, `burst` (default `limit`) at once.

```ts
redisFieldLimit({ url, limit: 30, windowMs: 60_000 });
```

## redisFieldLimit: burst × windowMs must be at most 9007199254740

The Redis script counts `burst × windowMs` exactly, so the product stays under `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER / 1000`. A
`windowMs` in microseconds or a huge `burst` gets there; lower one of them.

## redisFieldLimit: an empty bucket would take over ten years to refill

`burst × windowMs ÷ limit` is over ten years (a `GraxiaConfigError`). Usually `windowMs` is not in milliseconds (a
duration in seconds multiplied twice, a timestamp), or `limit` is tiny against a large `burst`. Fix the unit or raise `limit`.

## redisFieldLimit: timeoutMs must be an integer of 1 or more

`timeoutMs` (default 1000) is how long one check waits for Redis, connecting included, before it fails open. Pass whole
milliseconds of 1 or more, or leave it out.
